text: A Scrawled Note From Laertes

Father,

As I was preparing for my journey last night, I attempted to find a certain lute of mine which was the favorite among my collection. It has gone missing from its case. I'm certain Hamlet stole it. If you could somehow arrange its return during my absence, I would be overjoyed. Please don't hesitate to get Bernardo involved.

All my love, Laertes
Elise's Final Words

I am Elise, lady to the Queen, servant all my life. They say I am mad with fever. But this is truth. Hear my final story, if you are able, if you care a whit, if you can know its significance.

I was barely more than a child myself when Simona was first let into the castle, a glowing vision of a girl dressed in a peasant's rags. Even then the head scullery maid ordered her hair be covered so she didn't attract 'attention'. In the end, it made no difference.

Simona was kind to me. This, I recall. I often helped the girl with her work as she braided the Queen's hair. After she was finished, Queen Astrid would beg her to stay, to tell stories. Simona had a way with stories. She never refused. And when King Alexander came to bed and woo Simona, who was she to refuse him, either?

Then there was the book. That horrid book... Simona brought it home. From where? Who gave it to her? I still don't know. Four days later, news of Queen Astrid's sudden death shocked the castle into mute horror, and Simona was quietly whisked away to the King's chambers. She was now the King's only lover. A low-born nobody with the power to rule nations.

The guards whispered of Queen Astrid's body: of how she died with her own nails lodged in her throat, the flesh torn, gone abruptly and thoroughly mad, her blood seeping through the keep tower's floor.

Simona came to me early one morning when it was still dark, inconsolably upset and without a light. "The book is cursed," She whispered to me in the darkness, her face wet with tears. "Elise, you don't understand. I was trapped in Elsinore for ever, for a thousand years or more. I saw every outcome I could, every possible version of this world, and it was all rotten. What could I do, Elise? What could I do? The book made me choose, and I chose to let Astrid rot with it all, so I could rule..."

She kissed me goodbye and pressed a coin into my hand. "I cannot hide from God," she said. "But I cannot stay in Elsinore. Tell no one where I went. Promise me, Elise."

And here I am, breaking that promise. I know Simona lives. What happened that insane week all those years ago? What will become of little Ophelia and Laertes, and my beloved husband I left behind? I will go to my grave not knowing.

Should my family ever read this, know this: I lived a far luckier life than any woman of my station ought to have enjoyed. But the luckiest thing in my world was always you.
Queen Gertrude's Diary

May 2, MDXXXV

Tonight my husband seemed distressed. At first I thought he was missing our son, gone to Wittenberg. But... as the night progressed, he seemed to grow old before my eyes. He seemed... broken, somehow. When the second course was served, he collapsed while raising a toast—ironically, a toast to our health. I took him on my shoulders and bore him out of the great hall and up to his bedroom myself. 

As I lay him down in his bed, I noticed tears in his eyes. I tried to comfort him by kissing his forehead, but he pushed me away. "You will betray me," he rasped. "You will always betray me. Every time. You cannot do otherwise." 

He collapsed into something like sleep, then, and would not answer my questions.

When I returned to the party, our guests were concerned, but Claudius stepped in to assure them. "Everything's all right!" he boomed, in his loudest, most regal voice. "Everyone—Drink more! Don't take your health for granted!"

Then he turned and offered me his hand. "Now. I think a dance with the Queen will restore some life to this party. Don't you?" he said, smiling at me. It was as though I were the only woman in the whole world. In all my time married to Hamlet, he never once looked at me like that.

That evening, when all the guests had gone to bed, I found myself outside my bedroom door, saying my goodnights to Claudius.

"I don't want to go to bed," I told him, laughing. "I want the night to continue. Stop the dawn!"

"As you wish, my Queen," he said, and kissed me.

I was surprised at first. And yet—I wasn't. 

I kissed him back. He pulled my bedroom door shut behind him.

Surely I, too, deserve some happiness in this world that has been so cruel to me.

Don't I?
The Ravings of King Hamlet

Again... again... again... Polonius, not even you can save your master from Hell this time.

I concede defeat on ever finding that book. The Hand of Dionysus, they call it. I find references, mentions, breadcrumbs. Did you know it's been mentioned as far back as Judas Iscariot, and even older still? Polonius, find the book so that no one must suffer, must die like this.

Time is nothing. Death is nothing. For the last hundred years alone I have lain in the garden, awaiting the trickle of my brother's poison in my ear a thousand times. Again and again and again. How cruel should it be that this gap of time seems to begin and end with me lying in the garden on a warm spring morning? How does my brother always find a way to kill me? Is his hatred of me truly so strong? And my wife—my wife, her faithfulness useless, meaningless, the bridal bed soiled with another's lust...

Let her have him if she loves him so much. Let them cavort in the halls of Elsinore, and some year hence, the chambers of Hell. I could not say goodbye to my only son. My regrets burn in my throat like acid, like poison. I can say goodbye only to you.

So farewell, my faithful advisor. Bury me far from Claudius if it's the last thing you do. I can hear the playmaster's foosteps in the hallway, here to relieve me from this endless madness. I give up. I give up.
Hamlet's Personal Journal

June 6, MDXXXV Ophelia will not even look at me. My love for her means nothing now. And in the great hall, they rejoice my uncle's crowning, my father's proud form but a distant memory. If my uncle does not allow me to return to Wittenberg soon, I fear I will well and truly perish. August 8 That thing was not my father. It can't be. My father lies buried. But if it wasn't my father... what devil or evil spirit was it? Am I truly losing my mind? Was it real? Can I be certain it wasn't just a horrid dream? No, the others saw it too... even if they won't speak to me of it. My uncle cannot be trusted. Devils disregarded, there is yet something evil in him. I found the literature which Bernardo mentioned, tucked away in the gallery downstairs... it only confirms my suspicions. And yet... something in me keeps me from acting on it. What has stolen my courage?
Physician's Report, King Hamlet

...His Highness passed away last night, and my autopsy was performed this morning. The condition of the body is intact, with no visible sign of struggle or trauma... it would seem His Majesty died peacefully.

...As to the cause of death, the thickening of his blood at first gives the indication of a snake bite. He was slumbering in his garden when discovered, and of course, it being summer, there is nothing suspicious about being bitten by a snake, though it is most regrettable...

...However, upon closer inspection of the curdled blood, I detected a faint smell unlike any I had ever conceived of. And the bite wound is unlike any snake I have yet seen... very odd. 

...I am declaring his death an unfortunate accident under uncommon circumstances.
Flight of the Executioner

...And so it came to pass that the King of the Realm died one night, leaving his two sons behind. In this savage and warlike country, it was customary that whichever child inherited the crown for himself would immediately kill the others, eliminating further competition. However, these two brothers were twins, born within a scant few moments of one another. And so they brought the matter to High Executioner Selene.

They found her standing at the edge of the highest cliff in the kingdom, above the rolling and raging sea. 

"I am twenty seconds older than my brother," said the first prince. "Without any doubt at all, I am the rightful heir. Lady Selene, please cast my brother over this cliff immediately!" 

Lady Selene bound the second prince's hands and led him to the edge of the cliff. But the second prince sputtered, suddenly, "This is wrong! I may be younger, but my brother's body is weak and frail. He becomes sicker each day, and soon he may very well die. Then the Kingdom will be left with no heir at all! Don't kill me—kill him!"

Lady Selene paused to think a moment, then bound the first prince's hands, too.

The first prince spat with disgust. "My brother is a jealous imbecile!" Lady Selene wrapped a blindfold around his eyes.

The second prince stamped his foot. "My brother is a weakling and cannot see reason!" As with the first prince, the second prince, too, was soon blindfolded. Both of them continued to argue at the top of their lungs, screaming for the other one's demise.

Then the sound of Executioner Selene's fading footsteps caught their attention. "High Executioner, come back! You must kill my brother! I must be king! Where are you going?"

"I'm off to pour myself a flagon of wine and then pursue a career change to the next kingdom over, in that order," Selene replied. "Sounds like this one's gone a bit rotten. Good luck finding your way home with those blindfolds and binds on, lads."

The two men lunged at each other, unwilling to stand down. And the both of them went tipping over the edge, careening into the sea. The kingdom was none the worse for it, in the end.
Letter to His Majesty

Your Highness,

Indeed as I am in your employ, it is my highest honor and duty to obey anything you might ask, including the neglect of your father's grave if you so wish. Still, might I ask why you desire this so strongly?

Alexander was a mighty ruler in his time. Whatever horrors he might have borne you and King Hamlet—may he rest in peace—are no more. In life we are cursed to continually remember the flaws of a man, but when viewed through the mirror of death, perhaps we might look upon such a man's flaws more kindly. The Lord smiles upon forgiveness for difficult men.

Nevertheless, I will continue to ensure his grave is not cleaned and no new gifts are laid there.

With all fidelity,

Alard the Groundskeeper
A Sonnet for Gertrude

My glass shall not persuade me I am old
So long as youth and thou are one of date.
But when in thee time's furrows I behold,
Then look I death my days should expiate.
For all that beauty that doth cover thee
Is but the seemingly raiment of my heart
Which in thy breast doth live, as thine in mine.
How can I then be elder than thou art?
O therefore, love, be of thyself so wary
As I, not for myself, but for thee will,
Bearing thy heart, which I will keep so chary
As tender nurse her babe from faring ill.
Presume not on thy heart when mine is slain;
Thou gav'st me thine not to give back again.
A Letter For Her Majesty

My Dearest Gertrude,

I hope this letter finds you in excellent health. Although I have not had the pleasure of your company in some years, I hope you will remember me fondly, Aunt, as I do you. I write to you with news of your sister, my most beloved Aunt Margaret.

Not one month ago, as one of her maids served a meal, the maid happened to drop a glass goblet, causing it to shatter. One of those shattered fragments entered Margaret's foot, and caused her to take gravely ill as the wound festered. Her physician recommended the limb be removed, and Margaret, then in good health, bade it be so. Yet on the very morning she was to undergo such a thing, she passed into the arms of God. You will be pleased to hear, I am certain, that the sacrament was administered in advance. May God rest her eternal soul.

I know that Margaret would have wanted you by her side in her final moments. Take comfort in the fact that she loved you dearly, and spoke of you often in her last few days.

Your faithful nephew,
Charles
8 Signs Your Nobleman Is Treacherous

Have you often wondered at the true form and character of your lover? Pay careful mind: here are eight signs he's foe rather than friend! 

FIRST, within mere days of your acquaintance, he declares that if you 'call him but love, he'll be new baptis'd.' This nobleman is a walking source of dramatic show, clinging to any poor girl who crosses his path. Abnormally likely to meet his end in poison and tears.

SECOND, he uses the term 'taming' or 'shrew' in your presence—or even worse, in the same sentence. If he attempts to starve you to break your will, eat his heart out.

THIRD, he suddenly finds himself madly in love with your closest friend after promising you his undying heart. Keep a sharp eye out for faerie dust in the vicinity. 

FOURTH, he sticks a dagger in your back, then blames it on your 'ambition.' Don't worry: your restless spirit will have revenge. Stay indoors on March 15 if possible.

FIVE, after you help him murder his friends and cover up the crimes, he begins embarrassing you with inappropriate sobbing at your dinner parties. Even the most heartening prophecy can't revive this relationship. 

SIX, he tells you your wife has been unfaithful, but offers flimsy proof. Take a walk, enjoy some deep breathing, and stay away from pillows.

SEVEN, he tries to convince you to kill your brother. One might think this clear as day, yet this author is continually surprised.

EIGHT, sometimes he tells you to get to a nunnery. Other times he tells you he 'did love you once.' Which is it? Send this uncouth boy sulking back to university!
The Cleric Butler

MARCH This morning I awoke from a vision of God as I slept. I saw Him before me in all His glory, and He spoke to me. When the dream faded, I realized my face was wet with tears. The Lord told me to enter the service of a certain Duke Iocus living in a town near here, and to oversee the man's baptism. This particular Duke was orphaned as a child, and as such, his holy education had been sorely neglected. I knew I had no choice but to obey God's will and to go seek out this man. That very dawn, I packed my things, paid the tab at my inn, and traveled over field and hill until I reached the gates of Duke Iocus's estate. Duke Iocus is a man of notorious reputation, to be certain; handsome, but wicked. Of course, as I have sworn a vow of modesty and chastity, I knew his wicked vices would have no influence on me. I knocked once and, hearing a shout, interpreted it as an invitation to enter. Imagine my surprise when I found the good Duke himself in the middle of beastly fornication with a young maiden... on the floor of the foyer, no less. The two of them were braying and sweating as nothing I'd ever seen. Flushing red, I coughed politely to make my presence known, but the Duke merely rolled over and lazily extended a hand in greeting. "Ahh, a cleric!" He boomed. "What brings you to my estate?" I introduced myself and declared my purpose to him, asking if he wished to be baptised. He roared with laughter. "What rubbish!" He explained to me that he had no need for a holy man, but all the need in the world for a stalwart butler... and so, before I could think of anything better, I agreed to serve him in that capacity. "I warn you, my new cleric butler," Iocus swore, "I shall never believe in any God you serve." He may say this now, but I believe I can change his heart. APRIL My lord Iocus has kept me busy this last month. One of my continual duties is to ensure the sanctity of his personal bedchamber, especially its cleanliness, so that he might continue to seduce all manner of impressionable young folk into it at all hours of the day and night. His lust seems to know no boundaries. I find it both frightening and some matter of clinical interest to me. Today, when tidying his chamber, I thought I might leave my bible at his bedside. Surely, I thought, he might read a page or two? I was right. He pushed into my room later that evening without knocking and handed the bible back to me. "What a fascinating book!" he declared. "Have you come to know God?" "Sort of. I read only the book called Song of Songs. I learned so many fascinating ways to compliment a woman's breasts. Never read anything so erotic in my life!" "And what of the rest of it, my liege?" He shrugged. "Dull. Dry. Lacking in action, heavy-handed on miracles to service the plot. Couldn't get through half of it without falling asleep." He spun on his heel and left. MAY For the last month, my lord Iocus kindly allowed me to bring a prayer group into his home. It is but once a week, on the sabbath. Tonight's subject was on preparing oneself to enter the communion of marriage and opening one's heart to God. Three young women and three young men came to our door, all of them in their finest clothing, ready to receive the Word. Ordinarily Iocus is prone to leaving home on nights like these to drink and play, but tonight he seemed compelled to linger. Not one hour in, after the wine had been served, Iocus came to me. "We've nothing to serve them to eat!" he fretted. "Nothing but bread and cheese. What sort of a meal is that? My good cleric, run into town and purchase an entire boar at once!" I donned my cloak, took a satchel of gold, and started off, giving the group my apologies. ...But three hours later, I returned to a scene which disturbed me to my core. Around the threshold of the front door were strewn half a dozen empty wineskins. Entering the foyer, I saw two of the young women giggling and chasing after the lads—all of them naked as babes and red in the face. From upstairs, I could faintly hear the sound of distant moans. "My Duke!" I called out. "What manner of sin is going on in this home?" Six voices rang out in muffled, sensual laughter. "What manner, indeed. I can be as specific as you like!" Duke Iocus called back, the seventh voice, barely stifling his own laugh. "Though we're, ah, preoccupied. Friends, make room in the bath—I'm coming in!" I think I must have gone into a dead faint, then. I knelt on the floor and prayed with all my might. Later that night, Iocus burst into my chambers. His hair was wild, his eyes rolling. He was stark naked. "Praise God!" He shouted. "I beg your pardon?" I said, bleary and half-awake. "My dear cleric, I've seen the light! I want you to baptise me immediately. Tomorrow at dawn, if possible!" "My lord," I said in shock, "What changed your mind?" Iocus shook his head. "I was nestled in a pile of limbs and lovemaking for hours. I thought for a moment I might die entwined like that. And I did experience a death, of sorts. But then, at the moment of release, a sense of utter peace came over me, the manner of which I can hardly describe. I've never felt so content! So magical! So right! I remembered all your endlessly dull lectures about the Holy Spirit. And I knew then that surely this must be your God's way of speaking through me. This must be how you feel every day!" I stared for a moment in horror. Neither of us spoke. "...So you'll be baptised?" I ventured after a long silence. "Right away, my good man. I want to be a Christian!" "Fair enough," I said, and went back to sleep. The Lord works in mysterious ways.
May Eve

I remember Celeste rode in the front.

She was the head of the May parade, wearing a long white dress with a blue ribbon around her waist and flowers braided into her hair. No one had ever seen a May Queen half so pretty, they said. A trail of wagons tied together proceeded down the only street in town and there she sat at the very front, skirts trailing beneath her legs, which dangled off the wagon's edge. Her feet were bare and pale and clean, her eyes a blue to match her sash. And even I had to admit she was beautiful.

I watched her go by from just outside mum's cottage. She turned to smile at me and called out. 'Anna! Come dance with us!' She extended her hands towards me, the bells tied to her wrists tinkling faintly. We had been best friends once, after all.

But the boys who walked at her side jeered at me. 'Ugly little bitch!' one of them screeched. Another tossed a stone. 'Brown-toothed, slack-jawed, scruff-haired nothing!' One of them came after me with a stick, as though he meant to break it over my back.

Tears filling my eyes, I retreated into the woods. Far away from the raucous sounds of the May Day parade, everything here was dark and silent. The trees stretched like fingers overhead, and for a moment I forgot myself in that darkness. I knew not where I went, but walked with my eyes locked upon the mossy ground. There was no path. I needed none.

All humans know when they have truly become lost. And so I had. It was nearly midnight now, though it had been noon when I left my mother's threshold. A full moon lit my path, casting twining shadows on the forest floor. 

At last I came upon a still lake. And there I prayed to the spirit of spring herself, that great goddess whose image all May Queens were created in. 'Make me beautiful like Celeste,' I cried. 'Make me worthy of being the May Queen, too!'

The waters parted. A single wave lapped the surface. And then, slowly, the mare climbed out of the water's depths, one hoof at a time. It was a white mare, drenched through, and it shook its head wildly, flicking drops of water from its mane. Surely this must be the goddess herself, manifested in mortal form. Its mane was braided -- just as Celeste's had been -- but with mossweed, not flowers.

The mare stood before me, its golden eyes fixed upon me. At last it said (with no mouth that could move, but with a voice all the same) 'Child of man, have you come to seek my aid?'

'I have,' I said, quietly. 'I want to be beautiful. As beautiful as Celeste.'

It bowed its great head to me and nuzzled my hand. I touched it tenderly, its breath on my fingers. And, flooded with sudden relief that my prayer had been answered, I pressed my face into its mane and sobbed.

'Cry not, child of man,' it told me. 'Come into my dark waters and be reborn as a goddess in your own right. Merely climb on my back, and we'll descend together. You shall be a May Queen yet.'

I wrapped its mane round my fingers and pulled myself up her back with all my might, swinging one leg over her sinewy side. Together, we began to descend into the water. I felt the cold bite of it weighing down my skirts, my shoes; and before I knew it, the water was up to my chest. 

It was then I peered beneath the surface and my heart leapt into my chest. The mare was no mare, but a rotted, hulking thing, its flesh stripped in pieces from its corpse and fluttering in the water's current. The wet stink of death came upon me, and I gagged. I reached for the only thing I could grab -- a branch overhanging the pond -- and pulled with all my might. The creature ceased its descent beneath the water and turned upon me, its face little more than two shriveled eyes in a grinning skull.

A name rose to my lips, a choked scream. 'Brook horse!'

'Yesssss,' the thing in the water hissed. Its horselike lips pulled back, revealing sharpened teeth.

I turned to swim, but felt those teeth closing down upon my back. The moon grew small, high above the surface, fading from reach. The soft green of it all surrounded me. I sank down to the moss at the bottom. No. Not moss. Remains. And the last thing I saw was that sharp, grinning smile.

'You shall never be Queen,' it rasped. 'But your bones shall be beautiful indeed.'
Walking The Low Beyond

Hear me, young maidens who have traveled wild,
Whose eyes have never seen the touch of death,
Who tarry often when the sun grows dim,
Who linger long by cairns and caverns dark.

I once was you in spirit and in heart.
I am Persephone, the taken one.
When I was young I planted seeds alone,
And gathered flowers freely in the sun.

One day the earth burst forth with violent seams
And ashes belched with spite upon the land.
King Hades, Lord of Death, had come for me,
To seize and make me his unwilling bride.

At first I cried out to the world above,
But no one heard the call to grab my hand.
He pulled me down into the low beyond,
And I knew this was where I'd make my grave.

No flowers grew within the world of death.
I fell upon the ground and wept with fear.
As Hades offered me his outstretched hand,
I flinched from him and clenched my trembling fists.

He bade me then to take his hand's contents,
A small red fruit with tiny ruby seeds.
The god of many names, his countenance kind,
Pressed each small icy seed into my palm.

'Persephone, I'll never do you harm.
For years I've loved and watched you from afar.
Become my wife and you shall be the queen
Of everything that lives and moves about.

But if you wish to flee from me right now,
I'll trouble you no more and leave you be.
I brought you down here not to be your jailer,
But to show you the lands you might yet rule.'

Three days and nights I spent in Hades' world.
I grew to know his kingdom as my own.
When that third night fell on the river Styx,
I knew that I had made my final choice.

'I shall take these three seeds and be your bride,
If only you will grant me one small thing.
I wish to plant these seeds in darkness here,
And turn your endless winter into spring.'

So maidens, when you find you are now crones,
And when your kindest days all seem long past,
When winter sinks into your tired bones,
Prepare yourself to meet me then at last.

I'll guide you down the long unending halls
And bear you gently to the low beyond,
Where you will dine beside the ones you've lost
And join us in an everlasting bond.
Ophelia

That's me. As the child of a duke, I have some small amount of standing—but as a daughter, I can inherit nothing. I've lived here at the castle all my life. Sometimes I dream about leaving... but where would I go, and what kind of life would I have? Everything I know about the world lies within Elsinore's walls.
Hamlet

Hamlet recently lost his father, the former King, who was also named Hamlet. He used to be very popular among those his age in Elsinore, with a much more cheerful disposition, but he's changed--and not for the better.
Gertrude

The Queen is one of the kindest people I've ever met, and her people love her dearly. Gertrude isn't Danish, but married into the throne via her late husband, the King Hamlet. As is traditional, she remarried to the King's brother after his death—now she is Claudius's wife.

After my mother passed away when I was a child, Gertrude took Laertes and me under her wing. I've been eternally grateful to her for her kindness ever since.

Gertrude was born in Austria, and is a member of the illustrious Hapsburg family. In fact, her father is the Emperor Maximilian I. She's worked incredibly hard to learn Danish and eliminate her accent. I know she has a sister as well, who lives outside Denmark. Royal blood runs thick through her veins.
Claudius

Claudius is the reigning King of Denmark. As the younger brother to King Hamlet, when Hamlet passed away, he inherited the throne. 

It's hard to get a read on him—he's too formidable for most to talk to directly. He seems comfortable in his power, and wields it well, though many find him arrogant and repulsive.
Polonius

Polonius is my father, and the King's advisor. He can be a bit addle-brained at times, and he loves to talk—a lot—but he really just likes being around people, I think. He always means well. And he's been an attentive father to my brother Laertes and me... sometimes a little too attentive. It can be stifling.
Laertes

Laertes is my brother, set to inherit the title of Duke when my father passes. He's set to travel all of Paris, learning his music and experiencing the world. Meanwhile... I'm here.

My brother means well, but sometimes he can be a little intense. He's quick to anger, and even faster to act impulsively. Hamlet hates him half to death, but other than that, he's friends with nearly everyone in Elsinore.
Birgitta 'Brit' Brockenhuus

Brit is Gertrude's lady-in-waiting. She can be terribly cruel. We've never gotten along since she came to Elsinore three years ago.

She is the daughter of one of the most powerful noble families in Denmark, as with most of the people here at Elsinore.
Bernardo

Sir Bernardo is Claudius's right hand man, and the most revered soldier in Elsinore. He doesn't say much, but he's been my friend since we were children.

He earned his merits as a young soldier in the most recent war with Norway, riding into battle alongside King Hamlet himself. After that, he quickly rose through the ranks to prominence, and he's even got the King's utmost respect.
Horatio

Horatio is Hamlet's schoolmate from Wittenberg. From the look of him he can't be Danish, but I've never known his origin.

He served as a soldier in the last war alongside Bernardo, and from the way he carries himself he must be of noble birth, though exactly how I'm not sure. He's well-educated and eloquent, and always has something interesting to say.
Irma

Irma is one of the most feared women in Elsinore for her quick temper. She's fiercely devoted to the Queen, and originally followed Gertrude from Bohemia, where she and Gertrude were both born and raised.

Despite her teeth, I've seen that she has a warm side. She loves to gamble, and she's quite good; I wouldn't make a bet against her for all the world.
Marcellus

Marcellus has faithfully served Elsinore castle for several generations of royalty, and is a passionate advocate of the throne.

He's likely the oldest living man within its walls—he can be a little foggy at times, but years of practice with the sword have rendered him more capable than he seems.
The Hand of Dionysus

King Hamlet believes that if he had found a book - the Hand of Dionysus - he could have found a way to put an end to his plight. If this book exists, and is the source of this castle's curse, surely someone has to know something about it.
It seems clear this is the same book Quince had stolen from him long ago. If I can find it, then Quince might be able to offer some guidance on what to do with it next.
Lady Simona was last seen with the Book of Fates, and I know something King Hamlet did not: She's still alive. I can find her. Someone who sees a great deal of people on a daily basis might know...

Othello says Simona has been living in Castle Town all along - her identity hidden, I suppose, but it's easier if no one even suspects they ought to be looking for you. She'll return to the bar on Sunday afternoon.

Othello told me Simona returns to castle town Sunday, but Fortinbras's invasion of Castle Town begins before I have a chance to meet her. How can I push back the invasion's onslaught? Surely there must be a way.

I... found it. I possess the Book of Fates. So many pieces had to be moved in order for me to find it, but it now sits on my table. The book itself does not provide one exit, but many - and it seems Quince is far from who I thought he was.
Prince Fortinbras's Threat
Fortinbras' offer of peace was a ruse. Elsinore comes to a violent end when he and his men storm the castle. But now that I know this is coming, surely there must be something I can do?

Apparently Bernardo and Father have been convinced that Fortinbras posed a threat for months, but the King has been reluctant to act. They need more compelling evidence - some source close to Norway that could give me information.

With the help of Lady Brit, of all people, I was able to spy on Fortinbras in town and get the information I needed. I now know where in town the Prince is hiding. Perhaps Father or Bernardo could do something with this.

Fortinbras is in prison! If I give the War Council the information, Bernardo is able to find him and overwhelm him in town. As long as Norway's prince is in our hands, they won't dare mobilize against us. Could this actually work?

We almost had him! It seems if we suffer any losses, Fortinbras is able to take advantage of our internal disarray and escape. The invasion will still be delayed, but to stop it entirely... well, I'll simply need to keep everyone alive. Sounds deceptively straightforward.

I've... actually done it. The invasion has been held off, and everyone close to me survived! But it seems this is not a clean victory. The coming battles will drain on us and our nation. Is that worth it, to keep all my friends and family alive?
The Melancholy of Lady Brit
Brit has never been warm to me, but these days she seems especially down. I wonder if anyone has any ideas as to how I could reach her.

When I saw Brit and Laertes meet, she told him something interesting: she's been divested of her artist's tools, and hasn't received a single letter from her mother. My brother proposed Horatio could help with the former, and Her Majesty with the latter.

Horatio offered to help make new paints together in order to replace the ones that Brit used to have. Apparently he needs three components: charcoal, eggs, and linen. Pretty sure I can get some linen from my drawers, but I'll have to find a source for the other two.
I can get charcoal from a fireplace, eggs from Irma's kitchen, and linen from my own dresser. With them, Horatio is able to make Brit a new set of paints!
I can tell Laertes about Brit's situation, and he will agree to stay behind and check in on her. Hopefully, that meeting will go well.

Gertrude has been encouraging Brit to focus on her duties in the Castle, to the extent that she's been hiding letters from Brit's mother! She said something about 'where unheard wishes go.' What could that mean?
Gertrude hid letters from Brit's mother in the well in the grounds. Needless to say, Brit was not happy with them having been kept from her when I delivered them.
Unfortunately, it seems doing just one thing won't be enough to get Brit to open up to me. I'll have to figure out a couple different things to do.

I've succeeded. I had to perform a couple little acts of service, but I can sense that I'm getting to her. She said she plans head to the Castle Town bar, if I can catch her there, perhaps after we'll finally be able to talk.
Lost Notes, Now Ash
I saw Father burning some notes late at night in his room. What is he trying to hide?

I've learned that by telling others about the burned documents, Father will be imprisoned, but I'm still no closer to learning about what those notes contain. I wonder if there's something I'm missing which might help me here.

I met King Hamlet's ghost. King Hamlet's memories are fragmented, but he did give me a lead. My father is in possession of some notes, the King's last words, which contain some crucial but important knowledge. And although my father believes he must destroy them, the ghost claims he's wrong. Now that I know for certain that they were written by King Hamlet, that changes things.

The spirit says my father is in posession of his notes, and it's clear that these are the same notes my father will burn Thursday evening in his chambers. I have to find a way to stop them from being destroyed.

I had to do something truly monstrous in order to get my hands on the King's notes... but I found them nonetheless. Father will be safe and well in the next world. It doesn't make what happened right, but I know now his death is but a passing trial. Now all that's left is to speak to the ghost.
A Missing Lute

I found a note from my brother discussing a lute he believes was stolen. He thinks Hamlet made off with it. Laertes and Hamlet have always had a contentious relationship, to say the least. I wonder if I can help resolve this situation.

As soon as Hamlet and Bernardo had a chance to meet, they quickly realized that the lute was lost, not stolen. They expect to spend some time over the next few days on a wild chase 'round the castle to find it.

They found the lute. I suppose I didn't realize how far Bernardo and Hamlet had drifted apart over the years, and how bad things had gotten between Hamlet and my brother. All this time, it seemed natural to assume we were no less close than we'd always been, but time changes things. I wonder if it's too late for Hamlet and my brother to make amends. If Laertes and Hamlet could only meet, I know something good might finally come of it.

Hamlet returned the found lute to Laertes. At first, Laertes was furious, but I think the conversation was many years in its formation. It seemed to be cathartic, in a way; they understand one another better now, at least. Perhaps I can leverage this to help them keep the peace in the future.
Guildenstern is Dead

Somehow Lady Guildenstern's gotten the idea that she could pretend to be dead, and she finds it rather funny. So funny, in fact, that she's asked me to tell everyone she really is dead. This can't end well.

Rosencrantz, obviously heartbroken, planned Guilda's funeral as expected. At the very end, Guilda popped out and was... unpleasantly surprised at the lack of attendance. She's now decided that 'nothing matters' and 'we're all unimportant in the scheme of the universe' and other related nonsense. She's decided to plan a party for all of the other 'unimportant' folks in the castle and I'm invited. Insulting, yes, but I do like a good party.

I attended Guilda's little party, and at the end of it, I realized something horrible: She's going to die in earnest aboard that ship. They both are. And I have the power to save them. I can get on board and ensure Guilda lives. But first, I need to make sure I'm present when Hamlet and company sail for England on Saturday morning.
Guilda invited me to meet her on the foredeck. I wonder what she wants to discuss? Meanwhile, I need to find a way to avert this impending crisis.
I met Guilda on the deck, and there was a... moment, of sorts. I wonder, if we had more time together...
I met Guilda on the deck, and she called me her 'good friend' for the first time. She might be the first true friend I've made in Elsinore recently.

Guilda invited me to leave the castle with her and Rosencrantz forever. They want to gallivant around the countryside, selfishly forgetting and foregoing everything but their own worldly pleasure. Could I be happy, living such a life?
The Spirit

Hamlet and others have seen a spirit of King Hamlet haunting the castle. This is how he learned of Claudius's deeds. If the ghost is indeed real, maybe there is a way for me to meet it. Surely Hamlet knows something.
Hamlet is tight-lipped on the spirit - he needs to be sure he can trust me. He's asked me to get information from a diary his mother keeps in her room. Well, if it's what must be done, then so be it.

I've obtained proof that Gertrude and Claudius's affair started before King Hamlet's death. If I let Hamlet know what I found, I'm certain he'll do something rash. But if that's what it takes to understand what's happening, perhaps it's wiser for me to follow this to its conclusion, no matter what.

I've obtained proof that Gertrude and Claudius's affair started before King Hamlet's death. When I told Hamlet, he was fully consumed by his desire for revenge. He seems to have a plan he intends to execute during the time period when we would all ordinarily have gathered to watch Peter Quince's performance. I have a bad feeling about this, but if I want to meet this so-called ghost, I'll need to see this through to its end.
Some truly horrific acts occurred, but in the end, the spirit appeared. King Hamlet spoke to me. He waits on the walls each night at midnight. I've been asked to seek him out.
Irma's Ire

Irma believes Hamlet is in need of some long-overdue discipline, and I've heard her grumbling to the Queen about it. There's no doubt that Hamlet's been difficult for everyone in Elsinore to handle. I wonder if I can force the issue to a resolution.
I saw Hamlet and Irma meet, and the both of them fared worse for it. Hamlet was cruel and Irma only fed the flames. I sense something must come to a head sometime soon.

I can hardly believe what came of all this. Irma poisoned Gertrude and Claudius to death. Not intentionally, of course; she was trying to eliminate Hamlet. But she was summarily thrown in the dungeon. I don't want to think about what Hamlet might do to her next, but I feel some obligation to see this horrible world run its course.

Irma's desire to discipline Hamlet ultimately degraded into a poisoning attempt which took the lives of the King, Queen, and herself. The people I love are capable of such horrors. It's frightening to think about. But I feel as though I understand a little better some of the tension bubbling just beneath the surface. And there's a possibility... that what happened here might help me, somehow, in the future.
Claudius Coming Undone

King Claudius clearly holds a lot of power in Elsinore, but at a terrible cost: He killed his own brother. But what I don't know is why. What drives a man to do something like that? Maybe if I got to know the people close to him, I'd find out. It seems like the only person he trusts in the world is his wife, Queen Gertrude.

Reading Gertrude's diary, I feel like I peered through a window into her relationship with the King. I get the impression Claudius has spent his entire life chasing Gertrude, his sole confidante and friend. Now, at last, he has her. I wonder what would happen if he didn't.
Queen Gertrude passed away suddenly today. I noticed Claudius fled from the announcement. I wonder where he went off to.

When I found Claudius, he was a sodden wreck, out of his mind with grief. And then he asked if I would stay with him as he slept. A duty his wife used to perform. I'm not sure I like where this is headed. Ought I to pursue the matter further? After all, I need only turn back the flow of time, and it'll be as though it never happened... for everyone but me, of course.

I agreed to visit Claudius in his private chambers. And at the end of the night, he made it clear—in no uncertain terms—that he desired to be with me. This is a man I've known since I was a child. It's hard to see him as anything other than Hamlet's uncle. But in his offer there was some implication about the kind of wealth the love of a King can bestow.
Claudius gave me a gift: an heirloom necklace. It's the finest thing I've ever worn, and I'm afraid to accept it. He means to make some grand romantic gesture soon, I think.
Claudius asked me to be Queen, and I consented. All this in a matter of days. Men in this family line seem to move unnaturally quickly when their hearts are similarly moved.

Claudius and I underwent an official betrothal ceremony, to the utter surprise of everyone in Elsinore's court. In a scant few weeks, I'd be crowned Queen. I could rule this country, because the one who holds Claudius's heart holds all of him. Gertrude never used that power to her advantage... but I could. Is that right? More importantly, is that a future I want?
The Playmaster
I met an odd man named Peter Quince who seems to be a wandering actor of sorts. He's going to perform here in Elsinore Castle and has invited me to attend his performance.

Quince wishes to discuss something with me in private about his performances. His only requirement is that I've attended his play first, and then come to see him the morning afterwards in the Gallery.

Two things have become abundantly clear. The first is that Quince is outside the flow of time, as I am. And the second is that his plays are little more than cruel improvisation. He's decided to grant any request I might make regarding a subject for one of his plays. Judging by the reaction King Claudius had to the play about him, this might become useful to suss out more information from audience members.

I happened upon Quince in the gallery, where he and I exchanged a few words. He spoke to me about tragedy and referenced a tale I'd never heard about before. I don't know what to make of him. Is he teasing me or trying to help me, or both?

Quince performed a little side show in town, and it was odd, to say the least. If his story is to be believed, he's not only immortal, but some great godlike tool of his has been stolen from him. He's here in Elsinore to try and find it.

Quince visited me in my bedroom. He and King Hamlet's ghost are acquainted already. In fact, the both of them are outside the flow of time, like me. Quince claimed that I can find a way to stop the flow of time from repeating. But if so, how? The spirit must be connected.

King Hamlet's final notes mentioned Quince as 'The Playmaster.' He writes that Quince 'relieved' him of his eternal torment, which explains why he's a spirit in my world and no longer trapped in time. But if Quince has the power to do that, why hasn't he done it for me? What's clear is that all paths seem to lead to me finding this book--this 'Hand of Dionysus.' I'll need to do that before I can understand more.

He lied to me. He's been lying to me this entire time. He's no friend of mine, and he's not here to help me. He tricked me into fetching this book from Simona for him, and then intended to deceive me into using it so that he can have it back.

We did it. We killed him. We're free. We're really free. Is it over? It must be. I can hardly believe it.

The rest of my life begins today.

King Hamlet said it best: There will be no way out from this. The Playmaster cannot be defeated or outsmarted. This tragedy is inescapable. But within the confines that bind me, there is choice. That's all I have left to cling to.
Queen Astrid's Memory
In various places, I've heard mention of Queen Astrid - Hamlet's grandmother - but I've realized I don't know much about her reign. I could ask around to learn more.
King Hamlet expressed to me that his mother, Queen Astrid, may have also experienced loops. I've grown up hearing so little about her and her legacy. There must be more to find.

If I talk to Father about Queen Astrid, he acts evasive. Evidently, the Queen was quite close to my mother, and he finds it painful to discuss her. He mentioned that he visits her grave Thursday night, though...

I've learned that my mother Elise kept an account of Astrid's story... and it might exist somewhere. My mother contracted plague and was sent away to die in a sanitarium off the southern coast, alone and frightened, by King Hamlet. After she perished, her belongings—along with those of other victims—were brought back by ship and sealed in a small shed near the docks. Perhaps I can learn more information there, if I can find a way in.

The tale of Queen Astrid turned out to be a complex one, involving her husband, his mistress, Simona, and... my mother. I got help retrieving my mother's belongings from the shack on the docks, and the notes she kept were... strange, to say the least. Simona was trapped in a loop as well, it seems, but what was this about a book? About choosing to be Queen? And could she really have escaped Elsinore alive?
Gertrude's Chambers
The door to Gertrude's chambers is locked - but I won't let that stop me. There has to be a way to get inside. Someone close to her must know, surely.
I've tried asking around about permission to enter Gertrude's chambers. It seems as though only Lady Brit and Irma have keys to enter at the moment.

Brit agreed to lend me her key - if I set her up for a 'private rendezvous' with Hamlet. Well, if it's what I need to do, the task seems straightforward enough. I'll just try not to think about the consequences.

Irma tells me she would be willing to give me her key to Gertrude's room - if I organize a card game for herself, Lady Brit, Horatio, and Marcellus. I'll have to talk to each person she mentioned individually.

Gertrude's private chambers are always locked when time resets, but now I know how to get inside. The key is hidden in the shrubbery outside the Queen's door - if I retrieve that key, I'll be able to enter freely from now on.
To Catch A Spy
Bernardo suspects that there is a spy in Elsinore castle, stealing sensitive information and passing it on to unknown forces. I wonder who it could be.
There is a spy in Elsinore Castle, and I have to find out who it is. If I cannot, then come Saturday morning, I die. But where would I start? Who could help me?
Bernardo is running his own investigation, interviewing people about what they know. If I send people to him, perhaps I could learn something by observing the meetings he has with them.
Someone has suggested my brother could help, but Laertes leaves for Paris early Thursday morning. I wonder if I could convince him to stay?
I can convince Laertes to stay if I tell him of my fears before he leaves. I'm not sure what will come of it, but my brother is determined to unravel the potential threat. I should follow him.

Brit seems convinced that it is Claudius having me killed, because he finds my affection for Hamlet dangerous. It's believable, almost... but if Claudius wanted me dead, he's killed before, and wouldn't send another to do that work. Still, maybe there is something to find there.

My efforts paid off. The spy, and my repeated killer, is Lady Brit. She's been in Norway's graces all along. I've got to find a way to expose her before she slits my throat again. Now I just have to stop her.
Lady Brit is apprehended, locked away in a cell by Bernardo. Does this mean I've successfully prevented my death? If I make it to Saturday night, I'll know I have.

By turning Lady Brit in to Bernardo, I managed to stop her from killing me this loop. It seems my success might be permanent - I was surprised by a visit from Quince, who promised me Brit would never come after my life again. How he intends to accomplish this, I'm unsure, but for now—I wonder what else lies before me.
My Father's Death

Bernardo just delivered the news: Father is dead. Hamlet killed him after the play Friday night. I... am having trouble processing, believing that it's true. There is so much I would have done differently if I had known this was how it was going to end. I'll miss you, Father.

...And yet, that wasn't the end after all. I'm back at the beginning again, in a time where Father is alive. I've never been so happy to have him berate me. Maybe I have a chance to change his fate! I know that he was killed in Gertrude's rooms, and that Hamlet committed the deed. Seems as good a place to start as any.
I decided to try the obvious and tell my father what I had seen. He found my warnings hard to believe, yet he seemed to take them into account anyway. Perhaps that will be enough to save him.

Though my father found my warnings disturbing, it doesn't seem telling him alone was enough to save him. Bernardo just informed me of his death - again. I need to know more about how the events played out - and find a way to change the state of that room.
If I can find a way to access Gertrude's private chambers, maybe I can know more about the events that led to my Father's death.

I... I did it. I actually saved him. Though it did not come without a cost, it meant so much to me to see him live beyond a fate that previously seemed inescapable. I know it's a temporary victory - at the end of these days it will all be reset, and then he will probably die many times, just as before. But now... at least I know something can be done.
Prince Hamlet's Madness
Hamlet showed up in my room, raving incomprehensibly. He's been difficult before, but this is strange even for him. What could be causing him to act out like this?
I've been pointed towards the gallery—perhaps something exists there that could give me some clue as to the origin of Hamlet's recent bout of madness.

In the gallery, I found a clue as to Hamlet's madness. Apparently, he's been obsessing over some irregularities in his father's death report. Clearly, Hamlet suspects there is more to this story—but what is he hoping to accomplish?
It seems that Hamlet is concentrating most of his energy on putting on a play for this Saturday. Something's brewing. I feel uneasy about this.

Hamlet's actions and plans seem to have borne fruit—after the play, King Claudius confessed to God that he was the snake who killed Hamlet's father. The revelation was stunning, but Hamlet was strangely unsurprised... his actions indicate he already knew? Where could he have gotten his information?

Hamlet's madness was brought on not by love, but by a meeting with what he believes to be the spirit of his father. It's from there he must have gotten his information about Claudius's murder. But the information turned out to be correct - so does this spirit actually exist?
The Barkeep and Me
Othello, the barkeep in town, seems to live in a world separate from mine. I'd like to observe what his day-to-day life might be like.

The inn in town has been the target of a group of thugs lately, who are trying to extort Othello for more and more money. The situation is untenable for Othello. If the Royal Guard were aware, they might be able to protect him.

Othello has invited me to hear him tell stories... in private, after the bar is closed. I hardly think it's an innocent request, but I also find him respectful enough to feel safe seeing him alone. Father would be furious to know I'd gone without a chaperone, but... well, what he doesn't know can't hurt him, surely.

Othello told me the most incredible tale, and when he was done, he asked me about Hamlet. I didn't know what to say. Not exactly. But then... we kissed, and it was incredible. It still gives me shivers to think about it. What does this mean for my relationship to him? More importantly, ought I to go and see him again tomorrow, as he requested?

Othello told me the most incredible tale, and when he was done, he asked me about Hamlet. I didn't know what to say. Not exactly. He asked me if he could kiss me, and I turned him away. I don't think I can think of him that way, at least not right now.

Othello and I were together for the first time, in the woods. It was nothing like it was with Hamlet... he was gentle, but knew exactly what he was doing. It was the kind of quiet, intimate night I've rarely shared with another person, let alone someone unrelated to me. One of those nights when you feel as if you've known someone forever after just a few hours. Something large has shifted in our relation to one another. We were interrupted by Claudius. I've never been angrier in my life. How dare he try to tell me what's appropriate for me and what isn't? I'll do as I like, go where I will. Othello made it out unscathed, but I'm certain the experience frightened him. I ought to go see him as soon as possible.

Othello and I went to the woods together, and I showed him the castle... or at least, the fringes of it. And he taught me to swim. It was the kind of quiet, intimate night I've rarely shared with another person, let alone someone unrelated to me. One of those nights when you feel as if you've known someone forever after just a few hours. We were interrupted by Claudius. I've never been angrier in my life. How dare he try to tell me what's appropriate for me and what isn't? I'll do as I like, go where I will. Othello made it out unscathed, but I'm certain the experience frightened him. I ought to go see him as soon as possible.

I found Othello and apologized. He asked me to run away with him, to leave Elsinore forever and travel south. Quince promised me Othello was 'fated to love another,' but that we'd enjoy a good life together until that time came. Maybe that's enough.
The Prince's Ambitions

Hamlet asked to meet me in private, and confided to me that he desires to 'prove his worth' to me and rekindle our relationship. First, though, he believes he must complete some 'dark work' of his own.
The 'dark work' to which Hamlet refers is avenging his father's murder. He cannot rest, or become King, until that mission is complete. There are ways I could assist him... were I so inclined.

Hamlet came to me after the news of his uncle's death was announced. He's done it. He's cleared all obstacles in his path to become King. But will he be able to successfully accomplish all it takes to be named the official heir? I can help him. I can ensure he has the right advice. The next few days shall be a critical window in which to act to determine the fate of the country as a whole, and of Hamlet's life.

I told Hamlet I wanted to try again, with us. That things might be different this time. I truly believe, in my heart of hearts, that he's changed... but will it stay that way? What if he returns to the horrid person he's been all summer? I'll have to abandon him again, then, and I'm not certain what would come of it. But for now, I remain hopeful.

Hamlet asked me to marry him. To become Queen. I'd never dared to think about it before now. But I consented. I'm going to rule. And when I do, I'm going to do what dozens of queens before me could not. I know the cost of death. I know what it is to suffer. Under me, no one will suffer as I have. Never again.

Hamlet lied to me. He told me he wanted to make me happy, to honor me... and now he's gone and banished Laertes and my father, believing them to be threats to his rule. Is this the cost of this world? Become Queen, but lose my family? What a rotten, horrid trick to play. Even so, they might be happier outside Elsinore. And far safer. Perhaps all is not lost.

It appears to be the case that if I spurn Hamlet's advances, Queen Gertrude will ensure Brit and Hamlet are betrothed. What sort of world would it be, one where Lady Brit sits the throne? Perhaps it would behoove me to run this journey to its end and find out.

...And suddenly, my betrothal to Hamlet was formally announced. I think it came as quite the shock to everyone. This wedding is moving forward, at least in this world. Is this a world I would want to keep forever?
A Journey At Sea

Hamlet returned from his voyage to England, thanks to a bizarre scenario where pirates boarded his vessel and took him hostage. He believes there was a plot against his life right from the voyage's start. If I speak to the King about this, maybe I can uncover the truth of the matter.

I spoke to the King about the aforementioned plot against Hamlet's life. He seemed surprised and disturbed, but now believes me to be an ally of sorts. If I can only be there at the moment Hamlet steps aboard that ship, I might be able to find a way onto it myself.

I've made it aboard the ship. The King tasked me directly with ensuring Hamlet doesn't return to Denmark, and promised me a rich reward. I'm not certain I want any reward like that. For now, I'd like to merely observe and understand the situation.

Pirates. We've been set upon by pirates. Not more than a few hours after we left Danish waters, at that. Their captain calls herself Grace O'Malley, and though she may be coarse, she doesn't seem cruel. Perhaps she can be reasoned with.

Hamlet pulled me aside to tell me he's got a plan: when opportunity presents itself, he's going to try and overthrow Grace, leaving Rosie and Guilda to die. This is... worrying. I know there's a bloodless option here—or perhaps something bloodier, depending on how I push my luck. I'm dreading the confrontation.

I overheard some of Grace's men discussing her. Such interesting rumors. There's got to be more to find, certainly, and eavesdropping is my specialty. Besides, we're in the middle of the ocean. What else am I to do?

I accosted Grace in the captain's quarters about all the rumors I'd heard. To my surprise, she just laughed and suggested she teach me how to hold a blade. She's offered to meet me abovedeck and show me a thing or two. This woman is a whirlwind.
As usual, Hamlet ruins everything. That's all I have to update for now. Must go find Grace in her room and apologize. How embarrassing.

Grace and I spent the evening drinking and talking. She's nothing like I thought she was. And... at the end of it... we went to bed. We spent the whole night together. I've never experienced anything like this before. I only wish we had more time together. My heart aches for her.

Grace and I spent the evening drinking and talking. She's nothing like I thought she was. And... at the end of it... she asked if I wanted to go to bed, though I declined. Nevertheless, it's clear we're kindred souls. I only wish we had more time together.

We departed the ship just a few moments ago and were returned to shore via longboat. What a strange journey. I sense there are so many ways that situation could have turned out; I must now reap the consequences of my actions, or else return to the point when Hamlet and I left the docks and try once more.
I've agreed to join Grace's crew. I wonder what it would be like, if this was my final fate? To become part of her world of debauchery and action and see where that path might lead...
A Natural Course

No matter how I try to influence people, those I love get hurt. But I've never actually seen how events would play out if I didn't try to change anything. Perhaps I could learn something by just watching.

Even without my involvement, this all ends in bloodshed. Hamlet and my brother kill each other in a foolish duel, the Queen is poisoned, and the King run through. Fortinbras invades shortly after, and our leaderless castle provides no real resistance.

At least I can be certain than my actions haven't made things worse. They were always destined to be bad.
Find Laertes
My father is worried about Laertes' upcoming trip, and wants to talk to my brother before he goes. And of course, it falls on me to get him. Where on earth could he be?

By talking to Queen Gertrude, I was finally able to free Laertes from the meeting. King Claudius granted my brother permission to leave for Paris, but denied Prince Hamlet a similar request. Laertes wanted to meet before he leaves Thursday morning.
Get Some Rest
It's been a long day, and everyone is off to bed. I should go, too.
N/A
Laertes and Prince Hamlet are currently getting permission from the King to leave Denmark. They can be found in the Great Hall.
Laertes has to wait for the war council meeting to end, but I'm not sure it ever will at this rate. Surely someone at this meeting can intervene on his behalf?

By talking to Queen Gertrude, I was finally able to free Laertes from the meeting. King Claudius granted my brother permission to leave for Paris, but denied Prince Hamlet a similar request. Now Laertes wants to meet with me before he leaves.
Polonius urgently needs to speak with Laertes
Gertrude can sing
the party is happening
the guards have been acting strange
the court has been successfully informed
Hamlet is in a foul mood
Hamlet is staying in Denmark
they can't deal with this
Hamlet is paralyzed into inaction
I doubt they would be hanging out among the graves at this hour.
Here is where Bernardo reviews all his paperwork.
And, from the look of it, keeps anything he's confiscated from the other men.
'Philip Martin: he never could pay his bill.'
I'd no idea we buried debtors in the castle yard.
'Marcus Faber: One foot in the heavens, he followed the stars.'
Elegant and inspiring. Lord Faber must have been a dreamer.
'Max Grossman: Here lies a fellow of infinite jest, of most excellent fancy.'
Alas, poor man. I knew him well.
Someone has carved a heart around the names on this one.
'Kim and Dan McAuliffe: In death as in life, adventuring together.'
It's nice to see not all love is fickle.
'Christopher L. Morrow: Urge no more words; I have no more to say.'
There's poetry in that.
'Grace Kelley: Well, that could have gone better.'
I've asked around a bit, trying to figure out what 'that' was. But no one knows, or will tell me.
'Bryant Woods: No great loss...'
Sir Woods must have been serenely humble, then. Or dreadfully boring.
'Joanne Dragich: She thought she could find the cliff in the fog. Unfortunately, she mist.'
And that's why walls were built around the castle's cliff edge.
'Sarah Villegas: HOLD MY MEAD.'
Those were her last words. Some are ruminating on their meaning still.
'Kris Evans: Evs got sick and tired of rating: Died from an overdose of grading.'
Hmm. I've never heard of that device in the dungeons before.
'Jesse Schell: PERICVLA VERITATI SAEPE CONTIGVA.'
'The truth is often dangerous.' Would that everyone had learned this lesson.
'Sunny Hazzard: R.I.P. Sunny, too sweet for this world.'
The sweet are often the flowers that sooner drop their petals.
Yorick's grave. He was the jester when I was young.
He was buried in the royal graveyard at King Hamlet's request. The family was quite fond of him.
These are the royal family graves. The one in the center is Hamlet's father, King Hamlet.
Gertrude will soon be buried alongside him.
Some day, Hamlet, the Queen, and the King will all find rest here.
'Lady Simona of Denmark.'
The words on this tombstone have worn away with time...
On occasion, I like to write here. It's been a while since I had the time, though.
This is where I'd seat visitors for a chat... that is, if Father ever allowed me to have any.
It's locked.
That door's locked.
I ought not to leave just yet.
The guards have locked up their chambers for the night.
Leartes locked the door. I guess he wants his privacy.
Hamlet's locked the door. I should... probably leave him be.
The bar is closed. Othello has left by now.
The castle cutlery. Irma keeps it spotless every night.
All of Irma's various pots and pans.
One of the guard's beds.
It's... much less nice than mine.
Hmm. 'A Treatise on Divine-Given Morality.'
I had no idea our guard staff were so well read.
And there's a second book underneath. Oh, it's got illustrations in it.
What is that woman doing?
I take back what I said before.
When some new man joins the unit, they'll put their personal items here.
Playing cards, and winnings.
I'm surprised Marcellus just leaves this all out in the open.
Horatio's personal effects are here, what little of them he has.
He's not strictly a guard, but the King gave him quarters on Hamlet's request.
More convenient than staying at the inn down the hill, I suppose.
There are thousands of books in here. I could spend years looking through them all.
...Of course, some of them are so old they might disintegrate into dust if I touched them.
It's my mother, Elise. I think some travelling artist painted this for my father.
It's strange, but I don't remember her face very well... I only see my reflection in her portrait.
What's this?
This all seems so trivial...
But I can't stop reading.
Hard to believe Father has something like this in his room.
Ah. I borrowed this from the gallery some time ago.
It's certainly not a very uplifting tale.
I wish this story didn't feel so terribly familiar somehow.
It's a book of poetry.
Persephone... A girl taken from her homeland and made a Queen.
Sounds familiar.
This gate leads out of town to the countryside. There's nothing that way but a lot of fields.
Lady Edith, often called 'The Brilliant.'
She was renowned for her great intellect and keenly inquisitive nature—not to mention her morbid sense of humor.
When I struggled with Latin as a girl, my father often jokingly told me to come down here and ask this portrait for advice.
The late King Hamlet's portrait used to be here, but someone—Hamlet, actually—has gone and torn it off the wall. He's so strange.
We're so much alike, you and I.
This noblewoman lived long before me. Her name is rubbed off the plaque, but there's a bit of a poem scrawled onto the corner...
'My beloved hometown, the sweetfish river running through it...'
...Never could make sense of that.
It's a picture of a foreign castle.
'Wiener Neustadt, the site of the court of Maximilian I, for Queen Gertrude of Denmark on her birthday.'
Hmm. I suppose this is where Gertrude was raised.
Lady Gina of Denmark. She was known, I'm told, for her unfailing kindness.
Prince Max, a distant relative of Hamlet. His performance in hunting, jousting, and other sport was considered legendary.
I've always thought his portrait was rather handsome.
King James, I believe. A gentle king who was well respected in his time.
That portrait of Queen Gertrude was painted when she was just a little older than I am now—on the day of her first wedding.
That's King Alexander, Hamlet's grandfather. He's... intimidating. I wonder what happened to him.
Prince Florizel. Word has it that he fell in love with a shepherdess and renounced his claim to the throne to make her his wife.
King Douglas. He was a well-humored man and a scholar, noted for his many contributions to this library—among others.
He was a teacher to many, I'm told.
Hello, little one.
This one looks like it's been eating extra kitchen scraps...
That one's not very friendly. Nicked my wrist once.
Oh, I rarely see this one out and about. She's always hiding.
This one's grown large and happy. Irma must have taken a liking to it.
Bernardo and the rest of the guards have all but adopted this one.
She seems to like lingering in the guard quarters a little too often, hoping for scraps.
A sprightly little dog. I wonder whom it belongs to?
This hound's nearly always underfoot.
He looks awfully content. Wonder which flowerbed he's gone and dug up.
Hello, little hound! Have you been chasing hares?
Hamlet's gone and blocked out all the light. How juvenile.
If I want to sleep a while, it should be in my own room.
If I want to take a nap, it should be in my own room.
This is where the Queen has her hair done. A mirror of this size must have taken a long while to build.
Oh, Laertes... What could you possibly need all these blades for?
Elsinore castle looks enormous, even this far away.
It may look shallow, but it's deceptively deep.
I used to play here as a girl. Now, though, with all these heavy skirts... better steer clear.
These were carved, I'm told, after the last time Elsinore was sieged and rebuilt.
It's the Danish coat of arms.
It's late, I should really go to bed.
I have no reason to head to the docks right now.
That way lies eastward, out into the Sound.
Denmark controls the waterway here. All passing ships must stop and pay their tolls to us.
The Royal Fleet of Denmark is anchored close by. This harbor is rather shallow, so longboats come ashore to ferry passengers to and fro.
It's a note bearing the Seal of the King.
Hamlet's looking at it right now. I can't get close.
'I've entrusted these orders to two loyal servants, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, to ensure that...'
'...To be executed upon arrival.'
This is a death warrant for Hamlet, written by Claudius. It'll never reach England now.
Still, I wonder if... Rosencrantz and Guildenstern were carrying this letter intentionally.
My assumption is deception on all sides.
That way leads to the stables. Nothing in there but a lot of muck and mares.
That way leads into the fields. I can see the hills roll for miles. Regardless, I've no interest in leaving town.
If I knew how to steer a ship, I could go anywhere.
But as is, I would probably only wind up at the bottom of the ocean.
There's so little light in here.
This is where prisoners sleep. Or... try to sleep, I'd guess.
What just— What did we—
Is he... dead?
...It's quiet.
No Hamlet in my room this time. Something's definitely changed.
I wonder if Father's outside.
Still don't care for this place, even now.
Don't think you can fool me, Ophelia.
I see. It's the same as before. You're still here.
Still here? I was about to say the same about you!
You're going to miss the party. Everyone else is already in the great hall.
Your brother suggested we ought to let you sleep... but I'm glad to see you refreshed and ready.
Come downstairs when you're ready, won't you?
What's going on?
This is all new.
There's... it can't be. This must be another trick.
There's my girl.
Finally awake, O lazy sister of mine?
Ophelia! OooOOOoh, Ophelia!...
Uh, you'll have to pardon mother.
We all began drinking a... bit much waiting for you to rouse. The wine's been out for hours.
I'm so haaaappy! I love a good summer feast.
Now, love, can we finally begin?
I know you wanted to wait for Ophelia. Well, here she is. Let's not let the food grow cold.
Please. I'm starving to death. I'm not long for this world.
Guilda, we just had sweetmeats—not an hour ago, too.
But have you seen the table? Irma outdid herself. I can't wait another second! I'll die!
Finally, someone who likes to eat my food as much as I like to make it.
You all are having a party? What of the morning court session? What of Fortinbras?
Fortinbras? You mean the Prince of Norway?
What of him, Ophelia?
He... well, the... diplomatic effort. Didn't he... isn't he threatening Denmark?
What? Sire, have I missed something?
I don't think so. I'm not sure what you mean, Ophelia. But I have noticed there's no goblet in your hand. Hmm!
Come! Drink! Be merry! And that's a royal order.
Er, mother, do you need to be tucked into bed? You're drifting off.
Don't mind her, Hamlet. Let her sleep if she wants to. She'll wake up as the night goes on.
I'll watch over her, m'lord. I'll call for yeh if she wakes! Uh, assumin' I'm not drunk myself.
She seems remarkably happy tonight, doesn't she, uncle? The happiest since, well...
Since Father's illness took him.
Aye, she does.
I wish his health hadn't declined so quickly. I loved my brother. I wanted him to live. For her sake, and for yours.
It wasn't your fault. There was nothing to be done. Plague steals indiscriminately.
My father was a good man. And you—you're the closest to him I have now. All will be well in time.
I'll drink to that, nephew.
(This is so strange. Did history itself change?)
(Claudius isn't a murderer in this world, at the very least...)
Laertes. Aren't you sailing for Paris?
Oh! About that. for some reason, I couldn't sleep last night, and I got to thinking about it.
I believe I'll stay in Elsinore a while longer. There's time enough for travel later on.
How often does such a bright, warm summer as this come to visit Denmark, after all?
Well, that's wonderful. I'm sure Brit will be very happy, too.
Happy that he's staying? It's not the worst, I suppose.
(Listen, Ophelia. Just between you and me, I've got a little surprise in mind tonight.)
(Wait and see.)
Come, Ophelia. Let me show you to your seat. Shall we dine?
Of course.
Everyone, I've a toast to make.
Hear, hear!
Of course, Laertes.
I'd like to toast to health, to life, and to love.
And to this brilliant, wonderful woman—whom I love, and who has loved me in return.
Wha? Me?
To some, our relationship has been known a long time. To others, it may be—er—more of a surprise.
I'll say.
Why have I never heard of this before?
Laertes, you don't have to.
Tonight, I'd like to ask Lady Birgitta for her hand in marriage.
Ah! Yesh! Yesh!
Well, I'll be damned. Certainly took him long enough.
Laertes! This is highly irregular!
Oh, come now, Father. They're a suitable match of sufficient rank.
What have you to fear?
W-well, nothing, but I—I haven't spoken to or met her father, and I haven't asked his mind, and—
And well, the dowry, and...
Brit, I love you. I don't want to travel the world without you.
If there's any way you share those feelings... if you think you could... share your life...
I accept, you idiot. Of course. You didn't have to be so public, though.
Invite them all into our bedroom too while you're at it, why don't you?
Hmph. Well then. Let me not to the marriage of true minds admit impediments.
If this is your wish, then...
We're going to have a wedding!
Congratulations, brother. I'm happy to see you happy.
I must admit, I'm relieved. I wasn't sure how you and Father would take the news.
Let's not let the night end.
I've already talked to Bernardo and Hamlet. Whenever we can slip away, the three of us are planning to meet by the pond.
You want to slip away? But everyone's still here.
Oh, it's a welcome celebration, but I can only take so much drunk revelry.
A quieter venue fits the mood. You should come. It's been so long since the four of us got together.
Yes. I'd... I'd like that.
I'll be there.
This is it.
He's gone. I can scarcely believe it. Everything is the way it was meant to be.
Well, I'm going to be staggering back to my room tonight.
As well you should be. Tonight's cause for celebration.
And cause to drink to the death of Brit's taste in men.
You're just upset she doesn't like you.
It's quite all right. I've grown used to that unrequited feeling.
Not for her, though.
It's been a long time since the four of us were out here like this.
Too long. Why don't we ever have fun like this anymore? Did we forget how once we grew up?
I suppose so.
Well, I'd say it's the three of you who grew. I never had much luck with that.
Sorry, Wee One.
I detest that nickname.
As I recall, it was your brother who gave it to you. I'm merely reusing it.
That was the summer he called me The Ogre. Such an unpleasant phase for us all.
I can't help that I'm so terribly good with nomenclature.
I love you all.
I've been-- it's been-- I've watched you all die so many times.
I didn't know what else to do. I was so scared. So desperate.
But I finally fixed it. I was persistent. I did everything right. I fixed everything. And now you're here.
Everything's right again.
Ophelia? Are you all right?
She looks like she's falling asleep. She's not making any sense.
I can escort her back to her room.
No, no... leave her. She loves to be here by the pond. It's a warm night with a full moon. She'll be all right.
You know, ever since the castle's been in mourning, it hasn't felt the same.
I agree. There's been a terrible cloud over things. I'm certain that's what Ophelia means.
But today, for the first time, I had the thought that perhaps that period is coming to a close.
Perhaps things will be well again.
I'm starting to believe that myself, Bernardo.
In fact, I'll toast again to that. Shall we go find some wine?
Excellent plan. And some cards, too.
Goodnight, Ophelia.
Sweet dreams.
Oh. I'm alone.
Must've fallen asleep.
Wonder if the others are still playing cards.
Is that Brit?
She just passed out. In the dirt, no less.
Brit! Wake up.
She's cold.
No. It can't be.
It can't be...
Is that-- cheering?
Encore! Encore!
Yes, please! Don't keep your audience waiting!
I've seen this performance before, but I can't help but sit through it again.
I didn't help write this one, so I must admit, even I don't know the ending.
Look! She's here!
Quick, stop!
The others, outside. They're all dead.
Someone needs to examine them. My lord. My lady. Please.
What? Oh, yes, we know all about them. Disregard it for now.
Yes, dearest, leave them. The crows will get to them eventually. Or the dogs.
Now get on that stage, girl.
Ophelia, I'm so proud of you. If only your mother could be here to see you.
M-me? Get on the stage?
What's wrong with you all? People are dead outside. You... you don't care?
Ophelia. Start performing. Now. You're being rude.
Your brother's right.
Please, Ophelia, flee now!
What? I...
This is all wrong. It's all--
Miss me?
No! Nononono...
Why the pout, darling? Wasn't my retelling faithful?
My puppeteering of your family and friends... was the script not superb, the twist not sincere?
And I must say, your own performance was sublime. Well done!
What was it you just said, Gertrude, my dear? Do that line again.
Couldn't agree more. It was such an interesting strategy! What an odd way to play!
You thought you could actually leave the game board.
Just... slip a dagger between your opponent's ribs, get up, and walk away. How rude!
But that isn't how this game works.
Yes! Bring on the drama!
I am a god.
I have played thousands of matches across thousands of worlds.
There will be no winning in this game, Ophelia. Only suffering awaits you.
There is no secret way out! There is no magical solution, no solvable puzzle!
You will live on, trapped here, in great pain. And eventually, you will give up.
