Now take your seat on the opponent's side once more, please.
Fine. I found one way to kill you. I'll do it again.
But you see, I cannot die! Not really. I thought it might be fun to pretend to let you win for a while.
But now I'm bored of that game. And for your arrogance, we must extract a permanent penalty.
You. You're gone.
Yes. Go. Forever, this time.
Go to the little dark box where the game pieces lie when they're no longer needed. And stay there.
What did you do to him, Quince?
It no longer amused me, so I put the toy back where it belongs. Never to be seen again!
After all, naughty players get punished. That's how the rules work! And I'm just getting started.
All right, Laertes. It's your turn!
How can I help, Sir Quince?
You can die.
No! Laertes!
Stop it. They still feel pain. Even if they're only temporary fragments.
I don't care about hurting them. I care about hurting you.
Ahh! More, more!
Magnificent! What of me, playmaster? Is it my turn?
Thank you, thank you. You're too kind.
And... a hush falls over the theater at last.
So what's your assessment of this little experiment, Ophelia? Hmm?
Have we learned our lesson, perhaps?
A truly happy ending can't exist. Except inside your imagination, of course.
Or shall I force you to stay here in this world? I can bring them back to life, you know.
And kill them all over again. Dash their heads against the floor, have them duel one another...
There are so many fun ways! I'll even let you try!
There's one thing I can still do.
You can't control this.
Nothing matters. It's all useless.

Hamlet is the reigning Prince of Denmark. He recently lost his father, the former King, also named Hamlet. Hamlet and I were in a relationship once—long ago. He used to be very popular among those his age in Elsinore, but these days... I don't know, really.

Hamlet and I were together for two years, in secret. In that time, he was... different. Happier. He had a sense of humor then. Neither of us had ever loved another before, but he treated me with respect and an unfailing kindness. He went away to Wittenberg for University, and then his father passed, and he came back a changed person. These days, it's hard to look at him; all I see is the person he used to be.

The Queen is one of the kindest people I've ever met, and her people love her dearly. Gertrude isn't Danish, but married into the throne via her late husband, the King Hamlet. She remarried quickly after his death—now she is Claudius's wife.

After my mother passed away when I was a child, Gertrude sort of took Laertes and me under her wing. I've been eternally grateful to her for her kindness ever since.

I read Gertrude's diary. Inside, I found proof in her own hand that she began an affair with Claudius before her husband passed away. It's clear that she's been unhappy for some time now. Onerous though Claudius may be, he seems to treat her well above all others.
Gertrude hasn't slept recently. She's tormented by thoughts about her husband's death. It's slowly driving her mad, though she seems to do everything in her power to hide it.

Gertrude was born in Austria, and is a member of the illustrious Hapsburg family - in fact, her father is the Emperor Maximilian I. She's worked incredibly hard to learn Danish and minimize her accent entirely. I know she has a sister as well, who lives outside Denmark. Royal blood runs thick through her veins.

Claudius murdered his older brother, the late King Hamlet, and covered up his crime. He clearly carries an enormous amount of guilt over it and hasn't been able to find a way to confess. It's not even clear to me whether his wife knows, though she surely suspects.

When the King was young, his older brother used to beat him severely, so much so that he spent most of his life afraid of Hamlet. Is it any wonder Claudius despises young Hamlet, the spitting image of his tormentor? If someone treated me like that all my life... I'm not sure what I'd do to them. Every person has their breaking point.

Polonius is my father, and the King's advisor. He can be a bit addle-brained at times, and he loves to talk—a lot—but he really just likes being around people, I think. 

He's always been an attentive father to my brother Laertes and I... sometimes a little too attentive. It can be stifling.
My father is so loyal to the King that he's still keeping secrets on the King's behalf after King Hamlet's death. I worry it's going to bring my father nothing but trouble in the long term.

I recently uncovered that my brother and Brit are involved romantically, and have been for quite some time. It's understandable they want to keep the relationship a secret, given the various political pressured at play. I, er... stumbled in on them by mistake.
Birgitta ('Brit')

Brit is Gertrude's lady in waiting. She can be terribly cruel. We've never gotten along since she came to Elsinore three years ago.

She is the daughter of one of the most powerful noble families in Denmark, as with most of the people here at Elsinore. I can't speak my mind around her or my father would scold me for sullying our name.

Lady Brit is in the employ of Lord Fortinbras, at her father's behest. That's why she sought to kill me. Destroying me would ensure Laertes was angry enough to dethrone Claudius—at least, that was their hope. I foiled that hope in stopping her plan.

Brit has no desire to be here at Elsinore; she seems deeply unhappy, as though something's weighing heavily upon her. I wonder if it's possible to get to know her better, much as it would pain me to try and do so. I might learn what makes her so distraught.

I saw Bernardo performing in town today, as Katherine. I never knew. We grew up together, and I never knew. This doesn't change my feelings towards Bernardo, however she or he chooses to live in the future—but for now, the Bernardos in other worlds would likely prefer I kept their identity a secret.

Horatio was born in India, the son of a spice merchant who sailed between Venice and Calicut. He never knew his mother. He was raised as a Venetian, and at some point made his way to Denmark, which is where he entered King Hamlet's employ as a soldier. He's remained here ever since, barring the time he was with Hamlet at Wittenberg.

I've learned that Horatio left Venice, where he was raised, when his father passed away. He went to Florence after that and sought work as an assistant to master artists. One such artist was a man whose work he admired deeply; he became romantically involved with his master soon afterwards. That's the period of his life which spanned between his youth in Venice and his adulthood in Denmark.

Hamlet and Horatio departed for Wittenberg together, it turns out. King Hamlet sent Horatio to watch over Hamlet while Hamlet was in school, since Horatio was older and calmer than Hamlet. But Horatio and Hamlet became close, and Horatio told Rosencrantz that he's been in love with Hamlet ever since.

I saw Horatio mourning Hamlet, in private. He clearly has feelings for Hamlet which extend beyond friendship. He's been dealing with this alone, on his own. I don't think he'll have closure until he's able to find someone else to talk to.
Rosencrantz

Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are two of Hamlet's oldest friends from the university. I hadn't met them until recently—they're both the daughters of wealthy noble families, but come from foreign lands.

Rosencrantz is the louder and more surefooted of the two women, and there's a clear imbalance in their dynamic. Something has evidently made them inseparable, though.

I watched Rosencrantz offer Horatio some advice on matters of the heart, and in the process learned that she has only ever loved women. She seems to be rather open about this fact; I wonder where she comes from, that such a thing can be so transparent.
Guildenstern

Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are two of Hamlet's oldest friends from the university. I hadn't met them until recently—they're both the daughters of wealthy noble families, but come from foreign lands.

Guildenstern appears to be the more reserved of the two, and often follows in Rosencrantz's shadow. I wonder what she's like and what she knows about Hamlet?

The closer I've gotten with Guildenstern, the more I've realized something about her. She seems to be almost thoughtless and carefree at times, but she can be deeply, deeply kind. I think we might become fast friends.

Guilda and I shared a kiss late one night on the deck of our ship, after it had been overtaken by pirates. I wish we could have more time together. I wish I could get to know her more. Four days isn't enough time to process everything that happened.

Guildenstern and Hamlet had a brief romance of their own, it turns out. I suppose it must have taken place at school, when Hamlet was away. Perhaps that's why they were so quick to come to his aid when Claudius sent for them.

Guildenstern and Hamlet came to a confrontation when we were all on the ship together. It's still hard to make sense of it all, but she pointed out to Hamlet that he has a history of chasing women who represent some kind of exotic 'other' to him. Women like Guildenstern. Women like me. She's braver than I am. It's something I'd always wondered when Hamlet and I first began our courtship. Was he in love with me? Or simply the idea of a perpetual outsider who could never truly have the power to force him to behave?
Peter Quince

Quince is the leader of a traveling troupe of players that occasionally perform at the castle. He writes and directs every play the group presents. I don't believe the group has come to Elsinore in quite some time, so everyone's very excited.

Quince is far more than he appears to be, and has the ability to reshape time around him to fit his desires. Where did he gain this ability? He's offered me his assistance in solving my way out of my own quandary. I hope I can ask him about anything I might encounter.

He lied to me. He's not on my side at all. He desires nothing more than my total and complete destruction, as some kind of sick game—some source of entertainment for him. I cannot give him that satisfaction. I must push onward. I have the Book of Fates to guide me.
The Ghost
This spirit claims to be the dead King Hamlet. It wears his old battle armor and looks like him, and even has his manner of speaking. Not everyone is able to see it. A most strange apparition indeed.
Prince Fortinbras

The Prince of Norway, Fortinbras. His father was killed by Hamlet's father, and his uncle now rules Norway at large. Despite his claims of wanting to make amends, he has agents meant to manipulate the court.
Othello
The handsome and humble barkeep in Castle Town. He spends most of his days telling stories of far-off lands and performing songs for all to hear.

Othello told me a story from his life tonight. He has such a captivating way about him, almost entrancing. I find myself being drawn in, whether I want to be or not. There's more to him than meets the eye.
Othello's in trouble. He's being extorted by some local men, and he has little recourse to defend himself. I need to do something to help.
Grace O'Malley
Grace knows the waters in this area like the back of her hand, and hastily overtook us when we put out to sea. The fact that she spared our lives speaks to a shred of humanity in her.
I've learned quite a bit about Grace in just a small amount of time. She met the Queen of England, for instance, and was married twice to different men, both of them now deceased0 I believe.
Grace and I spent the night together. I hope I see her again soon-- or perhaps, if there's a way out of this repeating world, that I might accept her offer to sail the world.
This is the fate I choose.
How weary, stale, flat, and unprofitable seem to me all the uses of this world.
In the end, I come to understand what Elsinore truly is: a box filled with puppets. A street-show for fools.
Each day, the puppets come out of the box. A new story is told.
This one beats that one over the head, this one sleeps with that one.
The puppets are swapped for each new tale to keep it fresh and interesting, to hold the crowd's attention.
...But at the end of the day, all the puppets go back into that quiet, wooden box. All of it returns to the same point from which it began. And there is no escaping it.
Once I begin to see the frayed ends of the world, I can't unsee them any more. Once I see people as those puppets, I can't understand them as fully human.
All the love and hate I feel for them has vanished, to be replaced with... nothing.
I kill them senselessly, intentionally, with a catlike boredom I did not think I had within me.
Like a child picking apart an insect to find out what's inside it, I have cut down everyone in Elsinore to find out what happens when all pretensions fall away.
Now, Quince offers me something far more interesting: the chance to close the puppet-box forever and visit other attractions.
He asks me to come with him, to see other worlds. And I gladly accept.
It is far too late to do otherwise. I can't go back, not after knowing what I know now.
He opens a doorway in the air, a door which never before existed.
We step through, and we are somewhere else entirely, a world full of towering steel and screeching iron monsters.
And from there, a dozen more worlds after that. He shows me things no human has ever seen.
He treats me as his equal. He finds my confusion about these new sights endlessly fascinating.
I cannot begin to describe the places I go, the strange people and creatures I meet.
But in every world, the Book grants us the power to imprison them and pick them apart.
I've seen countless bloody and unnatural ends, brought on by lust, by greed, by compassion.
I've witnessed destruction wrought by the very stars themselves, which I thought once were mere fixed illusion -- until I'd been to them.
My curiosity is endless. With each day, I feel I grow closer to understanding the very soul of the universe. Its nature is apathy. Its cycle is death and rebirth.
And so we, too, carry on.
I once thought Quince was horribly cruel. Now I realize that the way I saw him was naïve.
I am glad to leave my old life behind. I had no idea how silly and simple it was, how utterly meaningless in the grand design.
I talked like a child, I thought like a child. Now Quince has given me the chance to put aside childish things.
Let us embark on this endless wandering together, this man and I.
Farewell, Elsinore.
Today, I am going to a lovely party.
It is being hosted by the Queen. She's been warm and generous to me lately.
She will come to mingle with me before the party, and we'll laugh together, discussing our plans for the night.
Laertes is home in Elsinore for good now, and he and Father will be there. They will come to see me at the party tonight.
Now that he and Brit are to be wed, I've caught him with Father debating the dowry long into the night.
Father will, tonight, tell Laertes all he once knew of love: How to be kind. How to disagree charitably. How to grow together.
Quince and his players will be there, too, providing endless merriment as the night goes on.
Hamlet and Claudius have made up as friends. Both of them will be there tonight, where they'll announce the first dance.
Hamlet will offer me his hand. It might have trembled, once, but not any more.
And when I take it, he'll look me in the eye, and give me a wink almost brief enough to miss. Then he'll pull me towards him.
This is the real Hamlet. The constant joker. The man I've known all my life.
As we move and spin, we pass Horatio and Bernardo—Horatio dancing with ease, Bernardo watching his feet in a panic. I stifle a giggle.
Against the wall, Brit nurses a goblet of wine and watches us with a small, quiet smile.
The night comes to its close by the fire, where wine and cheese are shared freely until we're all stuffed.
After I fall into bed that night, warm and happy, I wake to sunshine.
I dress and make my way to the pond. The flowers are in full bloom. Ours is an eternal summer.
No winter's frost can ever touch the pond's surface, or kill the hundreds of beautiful flowers which line its edge.
I peer into the water and see myself looking back at me. And at once, I shriek.
The Ophelia in the water is haggard; her eyes are sunken into the holes in her skull.
Her hair is a ragged mess, framing her face like a dark cloud.
She wears a white shift, and sits in a shadowy cell. Her nails are split and bloodied where she has scratched at stone, trying to escape the darkness.
Whispers come from the water. '...Poor girl.' 'Gone quite mad.' '...Kept here for life.' 'Lost cause.'
Slowly, they grow, increasing in volume and number, until the voices are screaming at me, booming through the water.
The Ophelia in the water looks back at me and begs me to reach through, pulling her into my world.
Her bloodied hand extends to me. But I can't. That would shatter the wall between us. That would... shatter... everything.
I rip my gaze away. The whispers cease. Above me, white clouds drift, immaculate in a blue August sky.
I wasn't hearing voices. I was hearing crickets. Crickets and frogs in the tall grass.
Everything is as it should be. I mustn't spend a spare moment thinking of that other Ophelia, the one locked in that horrible place.
I feel for her. But she isn't me.
Besides—tonight, I am going to a lovely party.
Laertes is home in Elsinore for good now, and he and Father will be there. They'll come to see me at the party tonight.
Quince and his players will be there, too, providing endless merriment...
Gone from Elsinore. My father's worst fear.
The gates closed behind us forever as we gathered into our singular carriage, all our worldly possessions strapped to the top.
We traveled for two days until we reached the outer limits of Denmark's borders - a small castle of no repute, crumbling away into snow and dirt.
This is the land my father was given to carry out the rest of our quiet lives.
We have no servants, no animals. Only these broken stone walls, and us.
At first, Father uses his connections to borrow a little money where he can. But he knows we cannot pay them back—and in time, that coin dries up.
We learn to do honest work. Laertes chops the wood that feeds the fire.
I gather what roots and food I can find from the forest to feed us, and learn to set traps.
For a while, it is a good, warm life, for what little it's worth. Every night, Laertes strums his lute as Father and I drift off to sleep by the fire.
I grow close to Laertes. I get to know Father in a way I never did. He talks about Mother more.
He talks about the love they felt for one another, and the love he feels for us.
Father clasps my hands in mine and swears to me that someday soon, he's going to get us out of here, somewhere better.
He says it with tears in the corners of his eyes, and I can tell he means it.
But one morning, after a particularly cold December night, Father wakes with a cough.
It does not improve. Soon, he lies in bed, unable to stand without shaking so hard he looks like he might collapse altogether.
Laertes and I bring him all that we can, every medication, every ointment. We sell a few of my dresses to bring the local physician to have a look at Father.
For the first time in my life, I pray.
I don't know who's listening, so I pray to Mother Mary. I beg her to keep Father alive, offer her anything she likes. Anything but his life. Anything.
And it seems like someone is listening to my prayers. Father's health improves, slowly.
He begins to sit up, a little. He begins to eat. We even take him outside when spring comes.
He begins to talk of us leaving this place and going somewhere better. South to Bohemia, perhaps, or even further afield.
But one morning when I go to rouse him, he is cold.
The body is stiff, eyes sunken, skin stretched too taut over the bones. I have to look away. Laertes holds me tight.
We bury him in a little patch of green moss close to the castle's walls. I try not to resent our exile as I look to the south towards Elsinore's walls, and... I fail.
After Father's death, it is hard to imagine ever being happy again.
Years pass, and Laertes and I frequently go months speaking to no one but each other. We are surprised to find we do not miss the company.
Both of us marry, eventually. Laertes meets a small woman with a gentle smile and a quiet nature—a shepherd's daughter.
She makes a pleasant counterpoint to his stormy attitude.
And I am married to a dark-haired man with a gift for poetry, a Baron's son.
Luckily, this one is far more kind than Hamlet ever was. Laertes offers him everything we have as a dowry.
Our spouses come to live in the crumbling castle and slowly, we begin to fix it up. There are new doors and windows now.
With all of Father's connections a mystery to us, this is our home now and forever.
A few chickens, cows, and pigs make do in the front yard, and soon they are joined by children, who like to chase them around.
This is not a noble life. This is not the life I would have chosen for myself, and it isn't the life Father would have wanted us to lead.
But in the end, we are—if not happy—something very much like happiness.
One woe treads upon another's heel, so fast they follow.
This is the way things were meant to be. This is how the story was always meant to end.
So what was I still fighting for? I no longer had an answer to that question, so I handed Quince his little black book and went to the woods.
When I arrived at the creek's edge, I came with fantastic garlands of crow-flowers, nettles, daisies, and long purples crowned all around my hair.
I wanted to show Quince that I was not afraid. That this was not me being backed into a corner, but emerging, triumphant, solution in hand.
The world of Elsinore is better off without me. And I am not afraid to die. Not anymore.
So I plunged into the water, feet first, eyes closed. It was only a moment before my skirts were drenched, and I was sinking too quickly to turn back.
Denmark will push on without me. Fortinbras will invade. The crown will fall. And all will die in the ensuing fire.
But out of the husk of this world, something new is reborn, because Fortinbras, that golden prince, is fit to rule Denmark in a way none of us ever really were.
Fortinbras leads the unification of Denmark, Norway, and eventually Sweden. The three countries unite together. For the first time in centuries, there is peace.
Fortinbras often speaks of the burning of Elsinore, that horrible catastrophe which claimed all of our lives. He uses it as a warning bell with which to rally all under his rule.
'Let us never have another Elsinore,' he proposes... though he was the one who shackled my country, in the end.
For once, there is little infighting. There is little to fear. The wealth of all nations continues to rise.
Those few straggling survivors of Fortinbras's invasion are permitted to remain at Elsinore and hold no court, where they lived out their lives in silence and mediocrity.
And no one within Denmark speaks of me, Hamlet, or anyone else again—save in whispers told to children too young to have witnessed the invasion firsthand.
No one remembers us. There is one grave into which they spill all our ashes. It sits at the far edge of the royal graveyard.
We bought this peace with our lives. I hope the future is a better one because of it.
I hope.
I join Grace's crew, and my old life disappears into the wake of her new vessel.
Life at sea is... unlike anything I've ever experienced before. One night the ship is rolling to and fro, and I pray to anyone who's listening I won't be thrown overboard.
The next night, everything is calm. The full moon shines upon the deck, and the other members of the crew teach me to play cards. We drink until my head is fuzzy and I curl up asleep belowdeck.
I soon become fast friends with the crew and learn about their lives. I'd thought them crusty and crude, but they welcome me with open arms and gladly call me their friend.
Grace takes up teaching me the ins and outs of using a sword. I'm a surprisingly quick study—soon I'm able to disarm even men of the crew who've fought for years.
I am not strong, but I am quick, and Grace says there's value in that.
The first time we are boarded by an enemy vessel, I freeze up. I nearly lose my head until one of my crewmates calls out to me, and I am able to find the guts to stand my ground and fight.
Afterward, Grace approaches me and catches me in a firm embrace. I never knew what it was to be proud like this.
We sail the world for three years, pillaging what cargo we might and selling it off the coast of Ireland to whomever will take it for coin.
When we're not sailing, we retire to one of Grace's coastal castles, and drink and flirt and tell stories.
Sometimes, Grace confides in me: about her past husbands, about her life before piracy, about her fears for her crew. She worries for them like a mother over her children.
We stay up long into the night together. We know each other more thoroughly than I've ever known anyone. I've never felt like I was home before now.
All of this comes to a sudden halt one morning when we are out far at sea. The day is foggy, and we are spotted by an English privateer before we see them.
We do our best to flee her, but she gains on us. Not long afterward, her crew boards our deck, swiftly defeats us, ties us up hand and foot, and lines us up on the deck.
They slit our throats one by one, or make us walk the plank for their entertainment. By that evening, only Grace and I are left alive—I have told them of my noble blood to buy us time.
There in the darkness, with our heads close together, I hear Grace crying for the first time in my life. I've never been so frightened.
She inches closer to me and, her hands bound in front of her, reaches out to clasp my own hand with her fingertips. I feel her hot breath on my face.
Then she whispers something I never expected to hear: 'I'm sorry. I'm sorry the adventure didn't last longer.'
The both of us lie there in silence, our fingers touching, until dawn breaks and our enemies come for us. They decide to slit our throats, too. I watch as they cut Grace's throat.
Thankfully, I only have to listen to the sounds of her death for a moment before their hands are on me, and I, too, am gone.
This life was a good one. Like Grace, I wish it could have lasted a little longer. But none of us know what time we have left on this earth.
I will never know what became of my family at home. Whether they were happy. Whether they resented me for leaving. I'm sure they did, at least at first.
But I made my choice. And it was worth all three years. Every single day of it.
I follow Othello out of town. He leads me to his horse, tied up at the last trough before the open road.
He gives me dun, rough-made clothes and a cloth to cover my hair and face. We both know I cannot be seen. I don't look like anyone else in town.
When the others realize I'm gone, scouting parties will be sent to follow in our tracks.
But they will give up around Denmark's border—and we are far swifter, traveling day and night alike.
Othello has a mind to head to Venice. As a massive trade city, it'll be simple for us to hide there. So we continue south; and I see lands I've never seen in my life.
I never dreamed such places existed.
On the path we encounter travelers. Sometimes they threaten us, other times they ignore us; but frequently they offer to break bread with us, together around a fire.
One night, we cross paths with a traveling priest. He is headed to a small abbey in the far north. He asks if we are wed; Othello and I look at one another and sheepishly admit that we are not.
That evening, the priest walks us through exchanging our vows. Binding our hands together with rough cord, he whispers a prayer over us.
I have never felt so loved, or so wanted. His eyes are the last thing I see before I fall asleep that night, his arms wrapped tightly around me.
....Othello, my husband.
A month later, we reach Venice. Enormous white buildings drop steeply off into the waterways, boats zipping to and fro.
It is here where Othello and I begin our new life.
I write a letter to Elsinore, addressed to just one person: Horatio. The only one of them I can trust not to come looking for me, in the end.
Several months later, much to my surprise, I receive a reply.
'I was once a popular man in Venice, believe it or not. Don't live in squalor. Let your friends help you. Love, H.'
Attached is an address for a tavern in the center of town. We visit it and inquire about Horatio; we are instantly given a small room in the tavern's attic, warm and dry and modest.
I am put to work serving wine and ale to the many soldiers and traders who call the tavern their mainstay.
Othello, having grander ambitions than pouring drinks, joins the Venetian Republic as a soldier.
At first he does as little as he can, and comes home to me by the time the sun sets each night.
But over time, he is gone longer and longer. He rises the ranks quickly. His commanders lean on him for his insight. And he has the sharp kind of mind and level-headed intellect that few men possess.
...One day, he is gone later than usual, and I run out into the streets to find him.
I don't have to go far. I see him standing in the middle of a marble square, calling up to a woman who leans over a balcony above him. Desdemona.
She is as beautiful as I imagined she would be. Her eyes are bright, and as the fading sunlight shines through her, she is radiant.
I see the way he looks up at her. I cannot hear their conversation. But it is clear that this is not the first time they have spoken. And it will not be the last.
As much as I speak reasonably, as much as I beg, as much as I weep, Othello has laid eyes on her... and everything Quince warned me about begins to come true.
He loves her more each day, and me less.
But that's the thing about human hearts. One moment, you can be as certain as stone.
And the next, with just a slight shift—one look of those bright eyes—everything has changed.
Eventually, I can bear it no more. I tell him to go, and to be with her.
And to his credit, he does not lie to me or beg me to keep him. He nods, kisses me goodbye, and leaves without another word.
But I stand alone. I need no one. I work at the tavern, and grow to like my small, comfortable, well-defined life.
I even grow to love it sometimes, in the quiet moments.
For years I loved a man who loved me more than life itself. A love to surpass the stars. A love which outshone even Desdemona.
I will never forget that love. But it's time for me to move on. And I do.
Venice is a magical city, a breathing, living city. It is full of art and life and God and the smell of the sea.
I find my own comfort here. At least it's not Elsinore. At least it's not Denmark.
But I made my choice. And it was worth it. Every single day of it.
No others were qualified to sit the throne of Denmark. It is time to let someone competent rule.
Who better than the woman who has seen all possible fates? Who else can have the power I hold?
I was once Cassandra, cursed to warn people and have them reject me.
Now I am Tyche, the goddess who makes her own destiny.
Fortinbras meets me in Elsinore's throne room, and for the first time we are able to speak as peers.
He agrees the war is senseless, so I cede him his little swamp, and we end it.
Let him have it. Let him have it all. Men's pride will always be the end of them.
Denmark is smaller now, certainly, but all the richer—as Norway turns its focus to Sweden and the two tear each other apart.
And all I had to do to avert that fate was listen.
The nobility are angry about taxation, about the flow of capital and power away from them. So I invite them to meet with me and I hear their grievances.
At first, they think me unfit to rule. They argue over who ought to be King among them.
But averting war with Norway is a point in my favor. Unproven though I might be, I am a Queen.
These days I am free of anger, free of ego or envy. I feel nothing at all.
I have nothing to lose. I have lost it all a hundred times before. And in that, the nobles find respect for me.
Claudius had moved to centralize power within the Danish crown and away from nobility.
But now, I establish a system of checks and balances to ensure all parties have equivalent say.
No king should have the power to sway a kingdom and begin a war as he pleases. I've already seen the kind of bloodshed which lies down that route.
Having earned their great respect, the nobility endeavor to work with me as much as possible.
We are able to enact incredible change. Things I never imagined possible when Claudius ruled alone.
Now and then, I hear rumors and insults. People think me cold. They whisper of the deaths which plagued our court, the deaths which made me queen.
They believe I ought to grieve more than I do. They wonder if a woman of my standing should ever have been made queen.
They wonder what happened to Ophelia, the girl—not Ophelia, the queen.
I know what became of the girl. Her future was stolen from her. She was forced to endure hell. And she came through it, alive but only half human.
Over time, those whom I called friends pull away from me. They cannot relate to the world I live in now, and I don't ask them to.
I must do what is best for my country. Even if that means leaving my old life behind. Even if that means I weather this alone.
Out behind the castle, a tiny row of new white graves line the small hillock to the north.
As the years pass, they, too, grow mossy and sink into the earth, joining the others. And memories of those who are buried beneath them fade into obscurity.
I do not go to visit them. I do not want to remember.
I do not want to run into those who remain. I do not want their faces to linger.
Living and dead comingle into a tiny box which I bury somewhere deep in my heart: The box of the Elsinore that was.
From now on, my life will be focused on the Denmark that will be. The great nation to which all others will aspire.
I alert the war council to Elsinore's undefended gates, and we are able to rally in time to mount a defense.
Rather than burning castle town on his way to the Great Hall, Fortinbras finds cohorts of men standing at the ready, weapons drawn.
And despite his best efforts, when he is thrown deep into the underbelly of Elsinore's dungeons, he does not escape again.
For all our quiet nature, when backed into a corner, Danes have always risen to defend our country with unrivaled ferocity.
Norway is deflected successfully. But not forever. Fortinbras must be returned to his people, and returned he is -- for a price.
But soon Sweden, emboldened by Norway's falter, moves in to attack us anew.
Claudius uses an impending war to turn his image around with the Danish nobility and summon troops from them.
So when all three countries clash in full force, our masses are equal. Across the salted cliffs leading up to Elsinore's walls, war rages.
And that fight, unceasing, consumes everything each country had, until we are forced to assume debts from anywhere we can.
Father, Laertes and I settle in for several long winters. We watch as Denmark's coffers are drained of gold, day by day.
Eventually, the war becomes a backdrop to our own personal hardships.
Things which had once been luxuries around the castle disappear overnight.
Hamlet is wed, with pomp and celebration, to Brit. All this for the price of more men, more horses, more coins from the pockets of the House of Brockenhuus.
Once-lavish feasts become a simple dinner of stew and bread.
We celebrate festivals quietly, internally, and do not throw the extravagant galas once common to Queen Gertrude's tastes.
At his wit's end, Father has my finest gowns sold to pay for a dowry for me, then offers my hand in marriage to the son of a wealthy family, a man whom I have never met.
But my husband-to-be is killed a week later on the war front. A dark-humored blessing.
Claudius taxes his countrymen to the greatest extent possible. They starve. We live.
We live. That's what's most critical, isn't it? We live. We wait out the rest of our lives, together as one castle, as one extended family.
Everyone survives. The first time Fortinbras attacked, I knew that was the future I wanted to see.
Through my own labor I was able to make it come true. I had that power.
It is far better to have survived, intact and unhappy, than to have died at each others' hands, right?
As long as we few are still alive... as long as my small tribe still lives... we can find some comfort in one another.
This life is not glorious. Denmark slips more and more into obscurity as the shadow of war shrinks away.
We are a poor nation. As long as I live, we will always be a poor nation.
Let it slip away then, into dusty books and faint memories.
I will make no choice. I will keep Quince here in this hell with me. Forever.
I cast the book into the fire of the Great Hall. It burns, but nothing comes of it.
When Fortinbras' men advance on Elsinore and time resets, the book is there, on my bedroom table.
Then, I clutch the book to my chest for weeks and lie in bed. Every four days, the castle burns to the ground. Every four days, I wake up again.
At first, Quince would come into my room and threaten me—scream—shout—anything to be frightening.
He would cast long shadows on the floor, or summon illusions to whisper my name.
Then, when I refused to do anything other than stare at the floor, he began to beg. That was more frightening.
To see such a powerful man being reduced to tears, a limp figure kneeling on the floor, clutching my hand and weeping...
But even then, I knew precisely what it was: A ruse designed to extract some pity from me. I have none. Not for him.
Elsinore is no more than a lifeless, empty shell to me now. I have walked its halls for what feels like a hundred years. Weary, stale, flat, and unprofitable.
I can never leave. And so long as I refuse to use the book, Quince can't move on, either. He needs it. He needs it to leave this world behind.
I will not allow him to cause any more pain, to hurt anyone else the way he's hurt me.
Even if it means I must endure the anguish he imparts on me a thousand times...
Even if he kills me and rips my skin from my bones, or turns me into pulp...
Even if he drowns me, or has me stabbed by my brother, or has my father tear my eyes out with his bare hands...
I will never up give this book to him. Never.
He can be my sole companion in this void of our eternal creation and destruction.
My companion... and my prisoner.
Hamlet and I have been formally betrothed, and as our wedding day dawns, I am awoken to be dressed.
A dozen maids come for me, bearing my gown, silk slippers, a thick white veil, and all manner of scented oils and tools.
They cleanse my hands, my feet, my body. They brush my hair and weave flowers into it. No expense may be spared for Hamlet's bride.
I sit there like a doll, allowing them to push and pull me any way they please. I am pliant in their hands.
They say... Laertes... has gone quite mad with fury.
After Laertes and Father were ordered out of the castle, they left. I do not know where they went.
I know nothing would have changed Hamlet's mind. Two decades of hatred and mistrust doesn't vanish in four short days.
I love my brother more than anyone in this world. I tell myself that his life is enough. I tell myself I had no other choice.
I try not to think of him somewhere cold and lonesome, hating me.
Once, I try to send a letter. Just once. I entrust a chambermaid, give her an entire pouch of gold for her trouble if she'll only take my scrap to the post in town.
...But nothing ever returns. I convince myself that Laertes read my letter but was unable to reply. It's easier to sleep that way.
One morning three months later, I awake, dress, and am led to the chapel altar.
There, Hamlet stands ready to greet me, resplendent in red and gold, wearing his father's crown. He gives me a slight bow and a smile.
I can tell from the glow on his face that he's never been so pleased to see me. Before him, a row of the most powerful men among the nobility sit watching—waiting.
They stare at me with cold eyes. They have no great love for this union. To them, it is a transaction to ensure the Danish crown remains intact.
And it is an uneven match, at that. The poor Duke's daughter. No true nobility. Not quite the riches they'd hoped to reap in making Hamlet's marriage.
They will always be watching over us. Hamlet is not a strong King—not yet.
They will drive his actions at every turn. We will never be free. I will never be free.
Before this wedding, Gertrude came to speak to me. She told me something I'll never forget.
She said... that there is no such thing as happiness one finds in marriage.
That this life is suffering from start to finish, punctuated by fleeting moments of bliss. Love merely stops the bleeding a while.
She's right, I think. Hamlet and I face one another.
Hamlet reaches out and takes my hand. He squeezes tight. The message is clear: I am not alone.
I hope I made the right choice, in the end. I want to believe I did.
I want to believe that this is the best possible world I could live in, with the greatest chance of happiness.
Hamlet lifts the veil from my face. We both turn to the altar. Light pours through the windows, passing through my gown and veil.
I feel ethereal, like I could float away.
After all, it's a beautiful day for a wedding.
The morning I depart Elsinore is cold and dreary. I do not know where I am being taken. The cart has been arranged on my behalf.
It is only late that evening, when my carriage arrives in a small border town, that I realize where I am going: Home.
...At least, it is my family's home. A small manor with crumbling walls, hardly an intact window, nothing to burn in the hearth.
It is all that remains of our house's once-great estate. Here I am to live out my life in silence, unopposed to our new ruler.
...And for two years, I do. I linger.
I sell most of my fine gowns and hire men to patch the windows and walls.
Slowly, the manor-home comes together. It regains its former loveliness.
But even when intact, it is not my home. It is my father's home, the one Laertes and I never lived in.
And nothing remains of Father here. So it can never be mine.
One day, a messenger arrives. I learn that the new Queen has sent for me—Queen Birgitta.
She claims she only wishes to talk, but... I don't know what to believe anymore.
I have seen Brit cut my gut open, spilling my blood upon the ground. And I have seen her kinder than I could ever imagine. So...
Rather than obey her summons, I flee. To the south.
I take little with me save for my only mare, her saddle, and some jewelry to sell.
I don't know why. Perhaps because I am a coward. Because now, if Brit slits my throat, I will never again have a second chance at life.
I continue south as long as I can. I make it eventually to Navarre; my mother's country, the land where she was born.
Here, in Pamplona, I blend in far better than I ever did in Denmark.
There are men and women as dark as me, and darker still. Song and dance fill every hall and doorway.
After one day in this sunburnt city, I feel my body in full relief. Yes, I think. This is home.
When I run out of jewelry to sell, I find work as a lady's maid at a splendid estate on the edge of town. My lady Margaret is a stern woman, but not unreasonable.
At night, I walk the lively streets alone. I peek in at every window.
I meander wherever my wants take me. I drink and I love whenever and whomever I please.
I take my time, a tardy explorer—like King Hamlet's spirit wandering the walls, like a fairy-sprite made of dust, never alighting permanently on anything or anyone.
Now and then I think upon the horrible fates all at Elsinore came to, in the end.
I wasn't able to save them. My family. My friends. Denmark has been thoroughly transformed.
I hear they've moved the court to Copenhagen. Elsinore Castle now lies dormant and shuttered.
But I escaped with my life intact, and that's what matters... isn't it?
At least, that's what I tell myself, when caught in lingering memories of those I left behind.
It is not a perfect life. It is far from free of hardship.
But it is wholly, thoroughly, blessedly mine.
Let them all tear each other apart. I'll be out having fun.
Rosie, Guilda and I meander from roadside tavern to tavern at first, making our way nowhere in particular.
Every day is the same adventure: What is this tavern selling? Who's telling interesting stories? Who is compelling enough to warrant a closer look?
And... I love it. I get to know Guildenstern better than I ever did in Elsinore. And I see Rosencrantz through new eyes, too.
When we run out of gold, they seem to conjure it up as though by magic. They'll do just about anything for a bit of coin.
Anything to keep us on the move. To where? Where are we going? It doesn't matter. I'm drunk, and I don't even care where we are.
Whenever I see Quince's maddening grin before me in my mind's eye, I drink, and it disappears.
Whenever I think about my father's corpse stuffed under a staircase, I drink, and it's gone.

Very convincing stageplay.

Bernardo—Katherine—whomever you desire to be...

My sweet.

Agreed. Shall we go?

When we last left Ophelia, she was ready to use the Book of Fates to remain in a perfect place forever.

The Mirthful Merchant.
Once there was a strange little man who collected and sold strange little trinkets.
Of course, the toys weren't strange to him. For every strange thing is beloved unto someone else.

Every man, woman, and child who received a gift had to laugh, in a lopsided, crooked way.
...For they had been given the gift most incompatible with them, and that brought them a perverse joy.

He moved through the world in a fog, handing out his gifts, collecting some others here and there, bearing a solemn wish of his own...
The wish to die.

The tide came up and washed over his face. Even still, he did not move.
The tide grew powerful and swept his bag of trinkets out to sea. But still—he did not move!

He felt his soul rise like the last lingering air bubble, shifting and squirming in the muck of the ocean floor.

Each of these stories would take on a life of its own. In this way, he was not just condemned to live forever—no—he must create life.

Brutally taken, and hidden. He searched the land far and wide, but even after many decades passed, he... found nothing at all.
And so, unable to move on, he languished. He could no longer create beautiful stories. His master's tool had been taken away.
Meanwhile, the ripples of his lost trinket were felt by all those around him. He felt its gift upon them—the gift of eternal life—but to them, it was no gift at all.
It was a terrible curse.
That is the end of our tale.

Aye. Everything in this area, an' things outside this map's boundaries.
You mean the New World?
Wah hah hah! Of course! An' a couple things you wouldn't find on any map, save for the truly good ones.
What sorts of places do you mean?
Well. Where shall I begin? How about th'time we were washed out on a strong current an' decided to visit the frozen Snelandia...
Truly? I've heard of it, but I thought that wasn't a real place.
Of course it's real! An' your people settled it!
As I said, it all began when we were washed out on a strong current with no wind fer days...
...An' that's when I realized, it wasn't another ship at all.
It wos a cliff!
Barely got out o' there wiv' both my hands an' my head attached.
I can hardly believe this is the kind of life you live.
It scarcely seems real.
Hmph. Yer sharp. You'd do well in it, too.
There's still so much I don't know about the world.
And talking to you, I realize... I may never get to see it all.
Well, perhaps between now an' Dublin, we can find a few new experiences for you.
Always more fun to show someone else th'things you love when they 'aven't done them before.
Speaking of which...
Earlier, yeh looked surprised when I said I prefer women.
I can show you a few things I almos' guarantee yeh haven't done before.
My new bunk's decidedly roomy. Danish shipwrights know how t'build comfort.
Spend the night in Grace's bed?
I'd like that.
My intuition's never wrong with th'ladies.
Now. How ought we to pass the time?
I don't think so, Grace.
Ah! I thought I detected interest, but my intuition failed me.
Well, I'll tell yeh what.
How about we tell stories instead? I only 'ave three livin' friends in the entire world, so for tonight, you can be my surrogate.
Happily. I could certainly tell you some interesting stories of life at court...
...I must have fallen asleep. Where has she gone?
Milady's consorting with the nobles again.
Think she relates to them better'n us salty old sharks?
Dunnah. I think she ought've killed 'em all on the spot.
She's still blue-blooded in 'er heart, no matter what she says. She's loyal to her first husband's family.
Lady O'Flaherty! May Donal rest in peace. If only he could see what she's doin' these days...
Old Donal would be in for a shock, that's for sure. He loved 'is sweet, bonny wife. But that wife is gone. The Pirate Queen took 'er place.
(I sense there's still more I can learn if I listen in a bit longer.)
(Grace hasn't called me out yet. Perhaps if I keep listening.)
I heard some of th'other men calling her the Lady of Rockfleet Castle last night. Do y'know why?
No. What's Rockfleet?
She married Sir Richard Burke three years ago today, and divorced him two years ago today.
What! Married for only one year? War har har... well, at least it was legitimate in the law's eye.
That's not all. Th'day she divorced him, she locked herself inside Rockfleet Castle, climbed to the highest window, threw it open...
An' called out the terms of her divorce!
The balls of six bulls, that one.
I'll bet she kept all 'is gold too. Isn't that right?
More'n half of it, by the time the divorce was complete, if I remember correctly.
Ruthless, wonderful, terrifying bitch that she is.
(Still nothing from Grace. A bit more should do it.)
So why're we all the way down in Danish waters, anyhow?
Didn't yeh hear about her meeting with the Queen?
Aye! I heard they're bosom friends now. Close as can be.
An' that she refused to acknowledge her as her Queen. There is no Irish queen!
Aye to that, friend.
So long as we don't attack English ships, we're in th'clear for the far future.
Any other kind o' ship is fine. Including Danish. And gold's gold no matter what flag flies over it.
Makes sense t'me.
(Grace met the Queen of England? The one who was asked to execute Hamlet?)
What t'hell are you doin'?
Think I don't see yeh skulking around, eavesdropping right and left?
If yeh want t'know about me so badly, you can come ask me yerself!
About earlier—I was merely curious. Your men speak freely of you when you're not present.
'M sure they do, the bastards.
Well, then. What have yeh learned?
That you've lived quite a life. Married twice. And you've met the Queen of England herself.
I may not look like it, but I was a lady like yerself once.
Grace O'Malley, daughter of Eoghan and Maeve O'Malley, Lady of Bunowen Castle, among others.
An' a fat lot of good it did me after my father died. Men swarmed in on all sides.
They took my hand, my home, an' my body. In return they gave me children, cattle, an' several hundred headaches.
After marryin' my second husband, I realized there was nothin' men gave me that I couldn't give myself.
An' I've been gifting myself nice things ever since. Ships, stalwart crew, castles... yeh know. The simple things in life.
It must be nice, having that sort of power. You go wherever you please.
So could all women, if they pleased.
No. That kind of freedom is not available to me.
It's... a long story.
I cannot leave Elsinore. Not at the... present moment.
But yeh've already left. Look around you, lass. I don't see yer castle nowhere.
We have different definitions of the term 'present'.
You're a strange little woman. I can see why the prince is so taken with yeh.
You mentioned their plans t'rise up against me and mutiny. I can't say I blame them. But...
Soon this ship will meet up with my regular fleet, an' we'll sort through what to do with you an' where you'd like to go.
Until such a time comes to pass, how about I teach yeh a thing or two about what it means to stand on yer own two feet?
I can stand on my own just fine, thank you.
What was that for?
You don' really stand alone, my lady. Yer stance is weighted all wrong.
Heavy towards the back, like yer afraid anyone yer talkin' to might kill you.
(Well, given the circumstances...)
Well, well! I'm almost impressed.
But bein' able to stay on yer feet will only get yeh so far.
So what? You intend to teach me how to fight?
It's a day or two o' sailing to Ireland. You think I can teach anyone t'fight that quickly?
Seven hells, no!
Best I can do is teach yeh how to hold a dagger. Let's start there, shall we?
Meet me abovedecks.
Ophelia. A word wiv' yeh, if I may?
What just happened... it could've been far bloodier. But thanks t'you, it wasn't.
If there's one thing I've learned, it's that unnecessary death always comes t'bite me eventually.
You may've saved me from all-out war with yer country.
My pleasure. Consider it all in a day's work.
Few have had my back in this life like that. An' the ones that have are on this ship with me.
When I find 'em, I like to treat 'em well and never let 'em go.
I believe you're such a woman.
Are you... is this... an invitation to join your crew?
Aye. But you'd never be able to return to Elsinore.
The life you had—that'll be gone. You'll need to change your name, your hair, your clothes.
Do you want to join us?
Join Grace's Crew?
Consider me your newest recruit.
Excellent. Then... crewmate Ophelia...
Yer first order of business is to get rid of that lavender dress. Burn it if yeh have to!
Gladly, Captain Grace.
My place is back with my family in Elsinore.
Thought you less bland than all that, but if that's yer choice, that's yer choice.
Get going then! And try not to regret it too much.
(If I do, I can always come back again.)
...So the others have gone. And I remain.
Murphy, set our bow towards Ireland. We're heading t'Castle Rockfleet for supplies and ships.
And after that—the wide an' wind-tossed summer sea!
Ophelia, meet the crew. Crew, meet Ophelia. She's divested herself of 'er genteel trappings, much like yours truly.
Hello, everyone.
Er, you all right, lass? Lookin' a bit pale there.
(I can return here—if I need to.)
The sound of the waves fades softly as I'm pulled through time.
Farewell, Grace.
See you in another life, perhaps.
This can't truly be happening, can it?
I can hardly believe it.
What do I do now, Guilda?
For the first time, I don't know.
I'm sorry, Rosencrantz.
Oh. Hamlet.
I heard about Guildenstern. I came to find you.
I came as soon as I received your word. I'm still stunned. I could scarcely believe it.
Guilda, I—I know it's too late, but I—want to apologize.
I was so cruel to you. And needlessly, at that.
All you ever wanted was to bring some cheer to this ugly, worthless world.
There are few who would do such a thing. You were a rare soul.
And I should never have discouraged you.
I'd stop you at every turn, shout you down...
No. What am I saying? She can't hear me. It's pointless.
I wish I'd said it before.
You know she would've forgiven you.
She always knew you loved her regardless.
I know you're right, Hamlet. And I was lucky.
I long thought myself fortunate to have two great friends in this world.
How times change.
Surprise! I'm not dead, everyone!
Wait... where is everyone?
Did no one come? Really?
...Not even one pity attendee?
More spirits!
C-could it really be a ghost? No.
No. This one's flesh and blood.
I can't believe no one came to my funeral. I don't understand!
This was... a prank?
Guilda, I'm going to strangle you.
How dare you—
You're an idiot.
How dare you be cruel like that? Ugh. I'm leaving.
Rosie! Wait!
Now you've really made a fool of yourself, Guildenstern.
This is definitely the worst funeral I've ever had.
Well. I suppose I really don't matter in the scheme of things, after all.
Just a tragic side character in the play of life!
A poor player who struts and frets her hour upon the stage... and then fakes her funeral, and then is heard no more.
But Guilda--pranks aside, your funeral was attended by those who truly love you. Isn't that enough?
Love me? Love is overrated. I want fame! I want entire harems full of fanatic admirers!
I want a monument with my name on it! First and last. 'Lady Gu—'... Wait a minute. What is my first name?
Oh, my God. Ophelia, what is my full name? That's how little I matter in the cosmic plan! I don't even have a first name!
Is anything real anymore?!
Er. You might be overthinking this a small amount, Guilda.
Phew. You're right. I just need to relax. See, this is why I keep you around.
Hmm. You know...
Perhaps this is a blessing in disguise. I think we should do something to celebrate!
Yes... how about a party to celebrate my total uselessness to the world?
The opposite of a funeral! A tribute to nothing important, and those who fall under that label!
I'll plan it. We'll have it... er... in the woods. Of course.
All good liquor-fueled binges start in the woods somewhere.
And you're invited, Ophelia! Who's less important than you, after all?
I resent that.
Ooh, bit touchy, are we?
Once we've all recognized our own worldly unimportance—well—acknowledging the problem is the first step in fixing it!
Welcome, one and all, to the gathering of those who are utterly unimportant!
I'm still peeved at you for your little prank earlier, but I can't resist a good gala.
I'd like to raise a mug in tribute... to us!
'Unimportant'? Can you please clarify for our benefit, Guilda?
Yes, do.
Well, of course, none of you are all that crucial to life here at Elsinore.
A bitter drop to swallow, but... well, I've swallowed mine already.
I thought we ought to celebrate ourselves, for once. And drink to our own health, because no one else will!
Nonsense! I've served m'lord's house faithfully since I was just a lad. I'm the most useful man in 'is retinue!
Hrmph. If yer lord finds you so useful, why does he ask you to guard the bedchambers and empty walls?
Because... w-well...
Don't answer it! Just think about it.
And drink.
Oh, an' I expect you think yer so important to th'Queen?
I'm an old woman. I've no time to debate my own importance to the world. Death is coming soon. For both of us.
Well, that's horribly morbid. Lady, I like your style.
And what of you, Playmaster? Are yeh gonna sit around an' let a bunch of girls call yeh useless?
Ah, my good Marcellus, how kind of you to call upon me.
As a master of the stage, my position is behind the curtains, out of sight and mind.
Therefore, I have little interest in this debate.
Guilda, I'm ever so slightly concerned about your mental state at the moment.
A toast to celebrate how useless we are? Isn't that odd?
Hee hee hee... not at all!
You see, when I realized nobody had come to my funeral... I was crushed, at first.
But after that, I felt—free. Free to do whatever I wanted, to go wherever I felt like going.
No longer afraid of death.
And if I die, I die. I won't know I'm dead anyway, will I? It's silly to be depressed by it.
I see. Yes, this is starting to make a little sense to me.
You know, I've found it a relief to be of little importance at court. With the rate at which this particular family seems to, uhm...
Encounter 'unfortunate accidents'...
I don't think I'd like to be of much significance.
Exactly! So let's drink!
And I'd like to give a special toast to Ophelia, who helped me realize all this.
Anyone got a deck o' cards? Could get a game goin'...
Heh! Play against me? Only if you're eager to lose everything in your pockets.
Yer on, old woman.
I'll run and fetch some. Guilda, won't you refill my glass?
How long was I out?
Um, an hour, maybe. The others picked up and left.
I thought I ought to wait for you to rouse. Although you did look cute sleeping.
The party went well, didn't it?
That it did, partner!
Hmm. It's rather late.
I'd better turn in for the night.
Ophelia... Thank you.
I... hadn't thought I'd find another friend before the end of my life.
But I have. I suppose that makes me a pretty lucky girl.
And the same for you. Good night, Guilda.
Soon, she won't remember me...
But at least she isn't aboard a ship to England.
I was able to change her fate... this time.
I'm certain we'll speak again tomorrow.
There's still time to save her, perhaps.
If I don't intervene, I know Father will be killed.
That means Hamlet will likely be sent to England, unless further circumstances deem otherwise.
If I can find a way to keep Rosencrantz and Guildenstern alive until the England-bound ship returns to harbor...
Maybe there's a way.
I'll need to get onto the ship first.
Who would have the authority to allow me on board, though?
I already know the King has the power to grant me access.
There's another option, too. If I can save Father's life-- perhaps I can keep them both safe from further harm.
I'll have to see what the next few days become.
By now, without my intervention, I know Father cannot be saved.
Oh, nothing. Rosie and I are leaving the castle, is all.
We have found Elsinore a most chilly welcome.
Totally unsatisfying.
Patently without class, poise, or even good wine.
Which would be all right, if the people were attractive...
But they aren't.
Well, except for you. And, I suppose, Hamlet. And... Horatio?
Certainly Horatio is a handsome man.
Yes, yes, we've debated this. Bernardo looks wonderful in everything. But I'm confident neither of them like women.
Lady Brit...?
With that attitude? Eugh.
Hmm. Yes. 'Eugh' indeed.
What she means to say is, we'll be departing shortly, forevermore.
And we wanted to bid you farewell.
Our everlasting thanks for saving us on the ship back there.
We'd most certainly have gone to a watery grave otherwise!
So, farewell, dearest Ophelia, you sweet angel of social manipulation.
Happiest of trails to you!
That is, unless...
...you wanted to come with us.
Oh, what a fascinating idea! You see, Guilda's taken quite the shine to you.
You're already color-complementary to the two of us, as trios go!
I'd love to. Let me gather my things and I'll come with you.
Let's be off, then, shall we?
W-well, I was in the middle of something rather important.
More important than us? Unlikely.
Come, now. Put that aside and live a little.
Back on the ship... you told me that time is repeating for you.
Back by the pond... you told me that time is repeating for you.
So simply come back and try it all again, why don't you?
You've got forever, after all. But this is our only lifetime!
Leave with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern?
(...She has a point.)
All of this—everything—has been so dire.
Maybe it's time I relaxed a moment.
That's the spirit!
(I could leave with them forever, now that I have the book.)
(Is this a life I could be happy with?)
We spent a long night cavorting and drinking at the pub in town. By the time the invasion inevitably swept through, we were all too inebriated to care.
I... can't.
Thank you for the invitation, but... I think I need to stay here, in Elsinore.
I'm sorry, Guildenstern.
Ah, well... your loss. I hope you have a splended life amongst the dour and dismal, my lady.
Come on, Guilda.
Goodbye, Ophelia.
(Perhaps in another life.)
How is her condition today?
I dunnah! Not improved, certainly. Still three kinds o' loony.
Ah, Ophelia...
Ophelia. Do you know us?
Of course. Perdita. You are lovelier than I ever thought possible.
And there's Florizel, the gallant prince, come to you at last.
Everything is lovely in the springtime.
Imagine me, gentle spectators, that I now may be in fair Bohemia!
The hills dotted with sheep, the trees all abloom... yes.
It shall stay so forever.
She's not comin' back, is she?
Not from this.
The Ophelia we knew is dead.
But she looks—happy. Peaceful. She's not in any pain.
Thank God for that. We've all suffered enough. Her, especially.
I wonder what her fantasy must be like. I wonder what she's seeing in there.
I just wish I could see that, at least.
I lie in an endless summer.
All right. Prepare yerselves for Irma house rules, peasants! No complaining, no shortchanging!
An' I'll watch the pot, of course.
And what's to stop you from sneaking off with the coin?
The fact that I'm a man of my damn honor, that's what!
Is the 'honor' part what makes your fingers so sticky?
Enough racket. Do you want Bernardo to hear you shouting and come running? No. I shall deal.
Tonight we play primero. I tire of Ruff and Honors. We play it far too often.
How abou' a little wine while you play, gents?
We... we're not supposed to...
The last time we drank before our shift, I ended up under the table, and Bernardo caught me and made me run thirty laps.
And I ended up in the bushes, and he made me clean all of his clothing by hand... even his undergarments!
Enough ninnyin' about. Let's play! You. Drink!
I've seen quite enough.
How long's she been hidin' in—I mean—ergh—m'lady!
We weren't doin' no harm!
Mmm. This looks awfully covert for a group who are operating above board.
Just give it to 'er! Whatever she needs. I can't run laps again like last time... my legs won' last another mile like that!
I'll meet an early grave if I, too, must run laps again. That bastard...
M-my lady, if you keep this quiet, I swear, I'll go against your father's orders! I'll let you into Castle Town!
Just meet me at the gates. Any time, my lady, I promise it!
Fascinating. Enjoy the rest of your card game, then.
My silence has a price, you know.
She's ruthless. What'd I tell you, Marcellus?
Just like her mother.
A-aye! Terrifyin'!
Just please don't tell Bernardo! I can't run laps again like last time... my legs won' last another mile like that!
Cygnus, I'll see you at the castle gates.
G-guard captain!
If you have time to gamble, surely you have time to train harder. Need I remind you all we are at war?
If you'd like me not to confiscate those, I suggest you spend less time mired in vice like a two-copper tavern wench and more time serving your ladyship. Now—go.
Honestly. I'm too lax on them...
Was I too hard on them? Are they acting out in spite?
I gave them everything! They just don't appreciate me.
(A gambling ring? So that's what the guards get up to in the evenings.)
(I doubt Bernardo would approve of this.)
Now is as good of a time as any to bring these supplies to Horatio.
I've collected what you asked for. Can you make the supplies you said you would?
Horatio, do you think if I gave you some supplies, you could produce some tools with which to make art?
Certainly. But I'd need some--
--Eggs, charcoal, and linen.
That's both eerie and unnerving.
So you'll do it? They're for Lady Brit.
Ah, of course!
Give me just a moment.
What are you two idiots doing? I have a permanent reservation on loitering here. Alone.
Actually, Brit, we brought you a gift.
I know you weren't able to find painting supplies here—so I've created some, with Horatio's help.
Now you can paint and draw again.
(...She still doesn't trust me. I wonder if there's something more I can do. Perhaps someone close to her knows.)
Might as well bring Brit these letters now.
Brit, I have something for you.
What are these?
Is this... are these... real?
They're from my mother.
Some of these are... months old. Where did you find them?
They were hidden inside the well on the grounds. I believe they were hidden there from you.
I see. Gertrude hid these from me.
And I thought I was the cruelest bitch I knew. Evidently not.
Mother wrote me every day, and she hid them from me. She lied to me.
Only because she thought she was keeping you happier by denying them to you.
Happy? The first month I came here, I wept every night, alone and afraid. How is that happy?
I heard nothing from my mother and thought she had abandoned me, forgotten me completely. Now I learn it was all a lie?
What kind of—she just—ugh. I hate Gertrude.
What kind of--she just--ugh. I wish I could... speak to her about this. To ask her why. But I can't even do that, can I?
Why won't you leave me alone? Why did you keep doing these things for me?
Why did you do this?
I want to be kind to you, Brit. I've been needlessly mean.
We don't have to be at odds.
I don't buy it. Get thee gone, you sniveling suck-up.
(...She still doesn't trust me. I wonder if there's something more I can do. Maybe I could find someone to help me.)
I told you to leave me alone.
What is wrong with you? You're like the thing that won't die. You keep coming back again and again.
I just—want to be—alone.
I know about Fortinbras. About your mission.
Yes, we went over this already. Though you still haven't elaborated how you know so much.
That doesn't matter now. I'm not here to have you locked up. I want to help you, Brit.
To the greatest extent that you'll let me. You can trust me.
W-what mission?
You don't have to act surprised. I'm not here to have you locked up. I want to help you, Brit.
Not here. Somewhere private. Come with me.
Claudius was supposed to die.
That's what I came to Elsinore to ensure.
Because my father thought, if Claudius were dead--
All this would be over. The war would end. Prince Fortinbras and my father would be appeased. And I could go home again.
As with many noble families, our roots run strong in Denmark. But Father believes Fortinbras will be a more sympathetic ruler.
Claudius has ignored most of the nobility's requests, even after I was placed here at court. Now my father and the other nobles want him gone.
The longer I go without succeeding, the more I just want to put down my head and sleep for a long time. Maybe forever.
But Fortinbras was placed under arrest. He's in the dungeon this very moment. What does it matter?
As if a prison can hold a man like that. He may be in prison now, but don't think for a moment he'll stay there.
His associates are almost certainly watching, just waiting to make their move and spring him free.
Hrm. Fortinbras's invasion... we spoke of it earlier. Do you remember?
What of it?
On the subject of domestic matters, I know Lord Fortinbras is going to invade Denmark soon.
I'm not certain how you learned that, but what difference does it make?
As I said before: leave me alone. We cannot be friends. And there can be no trust between us until this matter is resolved.
Now you know the truth. I hope it brings you boundless happiness.
Why won't you talk to me, Brit? Is something that horribly wrong?
I could, if you'd tell me.
I'm sure by now you've heard the rumors about a Norwegian confidante within Elsinore's court.
You're not saying... the spy... is...
Yes. Well, really, it's my father, but he gets his information from me.
My father is angry with Claudius. He's been trying to centralize power behind the throne.
He finds him unfit to rule, and believes Claudius misled the nobility about his intentions when they elected him King.
But if Claudius is murdered, everyone will suspect my father was behind it.
So my father plotted a secret coup.
A rebellion from within Elsinore's walls. Coax a man who already dislikes Claudius into offing him.
That man is your brother.
Laertes? But Laertes wouldn't attack the throne of Denmark. He's frustrated, certainly, but he's not a natural killer.
...He would be if you were dead. Everyone sees the love your brother has for you. It's unparalleled.
I don't know why I'm telling you this.
Maybe because you were the only one who'd ever been kind to me in this horrid place.
And whatever little it means, I'm sorry for this. I didn't want to do this. I really didn't.
You can still choose not to.
No. I can't.
Perished at Brit's hand.
If Fortinbras's invasion were rebuked, your father would have no choice but to work with the king.
And that might grant a more lasting peace than anything Claudius's death could provide.
But that's impossible. How are you going to repel a national invasion?
I don't know. But there's got to be a way.
I wouldn't have told you this before, but—Fortinbras is already here. Just outside Elsinore. He's been here a little over a week.
I've been visiting him. In town. He's staying in a small room with some officers, in civilian dress.
They meet late at night in the town square, long after all are asleep. They plan to meet next right before the siege begins on Sunday.
I can get you into that meeting. But you... can't reveal me. You have to pretend to be loyal to Norway, no matter what you see or hear.
Understood. I won't expose you, Brit. I swear it.
If you're lying to me...
I'm not.
Be there. I'll take care of the rest.
I know.
What? How--
It's a long story. But I know.
I'm convinced you're some kind of witch. Just haven't figured out if you're using your powers for good or evil.
In this case, it's for your good. Trust me on that.
Well, if you want to meet the Prince, he and I have a standing rendezvous.
But you... can't reveal me. You have to pretend to be loyal to Norway, no matter what you see or hear.
It'll end poorly for both of us if I'm there. I'd rather not.
You sound strange.
Call it a hunch of sorts.
Well, come to the meeting or don't. I'll be safe regardless. Blue blood is just as blue no matter who wears our country's crown.
Ophelia. A word in private, please?
It's nothing. I merely came to... thank you.
Claudius is dead. And Hamlet and I will be betrothed soon.
Claudius is dead. I'm hearing rumors that Hamlet and I are to be betrothed soon.
I thought you'd be happier, somehow.
That makes two of us.
This may be only a temporary arrangement. If Fortinbras arrives, I'm certain our betrothal will be disbanded as soon as possible.
And then, under his rule, I will become Fortinbras' wife. The Queen of Denmark.
But in either case, with either of these men, I should be overjoyed. I'm out of my father's hands now. He can't control me from the throne of Denmark.
I can paint any time I like. I can paint the whole castle if I so desire.
At first I thought this meant I was free—more free than I've ever been in my life.
But I'm not really. My ownership has merely changed hands.
I'm sorry, Brit. I wanted this to be good for you.
(Perhaps if Hamlet were betrothed already... no. That's a thought I ought not to explore.)
(I wonder if there's a world where Brit wouldn't have to be wed.)
Don't apologize. You've done everything I asked. And you've showed me kindness.
The invasion comes for us all soon enough, but when the dust has settled, I know at least that you and I will be all right.
With Claudius dead, Fortinbras has assured my father that Elsinore will fall all the more swiftly.

That scent. I know that scent. Hemlock.
Oh, Claudius. You've been a rotten, vile beast, haven't you?
And now it's time to pay for your crimes. The proof is in hand. What must be done...
And his desk is mere letters, too. All of it. There's nothing here.
Y-you mean—he cannot be—innocent.
There must be something else, some... real... proof. Somewhere. Musn't there?
Hmph. Locked. Of course.
But with a twist of the hand, a knife inserted there...
I smell hemlock.
And of course. Here it is. The fool would keep it in his chambers.
This is much too potent to remain in his hands.
I'll keep it for myself. Perhaps it can be of some use to me.
But this vase is empty. There's nothing here. And nothing in these drawers, either.
I let that fool of a girl run me around. Stupid, Irma. Stupid.
Ophelia. I found it.
In his chambers, just as you described...
It was the final proof I needed. Let me not pause further. Let this proof unstick me.
And what will you do now?
Take the matter to him plainly, without further ado. You'll see.
My heart is resolved for the first time in months.
Claudius killed my father. I feel it firmly in my gut. And he'll kill again if he isn't stopped.
We cannot let that happen.
This is further proof of my Uncle's crimes. However...
It took so much for me to be sure. I no longer know what to do. And now everything's become stranger than before.
Too much is already in motion. We have no choice but to see where it leads, now.
But I will take heart in having at least stolen one of his tools.
Ophelia. I found the poison you described.
I wish that I had not.
I'm sorry, my lady. I felt you needed to see it.
Deep down, I knew.
There were whispers after Hamlet died. Of the way his body looked. The... suddenness of it.
There are no poisonous snakes in Denmark, Ophelia.
But I turned away from it all. I didn't want to know.
Even then I realized the truth. There are no good men. We women see the wickedness in their hearts. And we ignore it out of love.
I will deal with my husband. I will smite this wickedness by my own hand. I owe him that much.
I will find some immediate use of it myself, I believe.
Some rats have been troubling the kitchen for far too many years. Eighteen, to be precise.
And one of them, the Prince of them all, has scurried too far out of his hole, making trouble...
Better to be rid of him as swiftly as possible.
I shall retain it close for now, Fräulein. At the very least, the King should not have it.
That vile man. I shudder to think what pain he might have caused my lady. Or perhaps it was meant for her. I shall never know.
What will be done to the King as a result?
I've dumped it out. He shall not use it to harm again.
But Bernardo, that doesn't stop him harming others. It merely removes his tool.
There's nothing more I can do, my lady. I'm sorry. I'm merely glad Hamlet and the Queen didn't learn of it. They may have... reacted poorly.
If you ask me, this has saved us all from a bloodbath.
I went to your chambers to find you, but one of the guards let me know you'd gone to town of all places.
Despite, if memory serves, my explicit orders that you were not to be permitted to leave Elsinore.
We'll discuss that problem another day, daughter of mine.
Regardless, I was... troubled to find the vial. I still don't know what to make of it.
And what do you intend to do with it, Father?
...It is gone.
I've dumped it out upon the floor. It shall never harm further.
Father, he won't hesitate to harm others. The poison's been stopped, but not the man.
My love, no one man or woman can stop a vengeful king. It takes a proper coup.
And we are both far too small to raise one of those.
Someday, you'll understand—how futile these things can be in reality, yet feel so close to grasp in the mind's eye.
Claudius? I'm unlocking the door.
What calls you to me, love?
It's been a week or so since we had time together like this. Alone.
...Yes, you've been rather involved, haven't you.
Shall we make the beast with two backs?
I know, Claudius.
And now that chasm calls out for blood.
G-gerta, you—you know how cruel he was to me. How my father hated me. You knew!

I am truly a fool.
I never saw it. All this time. I gave everything to Denmark, and it gave me nothing in return.
How could I have been so naïve? When Hamlet died, I thought with Claudius, things would be the same.
