Well, never mind it.
But these people see me as dispensable. Useless. Obtuse. Idiotic.
There's no longer any point to remaining here. My children and I should have left long ago.
This court has done nothing but take from us. My wife, my daughter's purity, my own dignity—I owe these people nothing more.
H-how long have you been listening?
Long enough to know that I agree.
You'd be happier away from all this. Living a simpler life.
Would you... resent me for taking you away from everything here?
Not if it meant you were happy and free.
...Oh, Ophelia.
I've been a horrid father to you, haven't I? Questioning your every move, hovering over your shoulder—
You and your brother are the only truth that matters.
Let me never forget that. Never again.
It's boarded up.
You see why I asked you, now.
Aye. But a good shove...
I heard cracking.
One more...
There. It snapped.
Is all well?
Come see for yourself.
Those are hers?
I don't think I can do this.
Everything's coming back. I feel ill.
I thought I'd forgotten her. It was easier like that.
Sometimes I merely pretended she was a dream, that she was never alive.
I have to go.
You don't have to be strong all the time, Laertes.
I know I was small. I know I don't remember her the way you do. It must be worse for you.
I don't...
I can't...
This feels wretched. I never should have come here.
Ophelia... this shack is already open.
Oh. Yes. So it is.
I... don't think I can go in there.
I'll leave yo to it.
You see why I asked you to come, now.
...And what do you expect me to do?
What men are good for. Brute force.
I heard cracking. Do that again.
It's given way a little.
I believe it's open. Perhaps.
Ophelia? Are you... all right?
Come and see this.
Are those...
I believe so. My mother's belongings.
It looks as though there's a journal, too.
Yes. My mother's belongings.
Do you... remember her?
Not at all. I have a thin memory of her face... but that could be my memory, or the portrait Father keeps on his wall.
She was very like that painting. And like you. I was old enough to remember her, a little.
I'm not... I've never been... good at things like this.

All of this was hidden from me.
I wish she could be here now.
Me, too.
W-well, then.
I'll leave you in peace.
I... don't understand.
This shack is already open. Is this some sort of prank?
Oh. No, no prank. I guess... I forgot? Laertes opened it earlier.
Ah. Forgot. I see.
Well, better he catch the plague than I, I suppose. Be careful in there, Ophelia.
Ugh! I can't even look at Hamlet!
There, there. Have a seat.
What can I get you two ladies?
The largest flagons of wine you can manage, sir...
Call me Othello. Done, and done.

It's her former lover. He's gone stark raving mad.
Did you see the way he was carrying on, Rosie? That strange, twitchy look in his eye?
He's certainly changed quickly.
Say, Rosie, you don't think he...
Absolutely. I was thinking exactly that.
But if that's true, then...
Oh, my goodness.
How dare he!
I cannot believe him.
Er. I've missed a crucial piece somewhere.
What are you talking about? Who is 'he'? What has 'he' done?
(And how do they know what in hell the other one's talking about...?)
W-well, you see, Guilda and this man... have a long history.
And it's not like him to act the way he did when we spoke to him.
He's hanging on to some secret. And we're not sure what it might be.
Or maybe we are, because that secret...
...Is that he's in love with someone else.
These things have a way of happening, my ladies.
Othello, what would you do if someone you loved found a new love of their own?
Me? Well, to be certain, I've never loved all that deeply.
I'd prefer to think I have a free and open nature. I think men honest who seem to be so.
Someone once told me I was easy to lead around, like a donkey...

If you love that person, then you love the very act of them loving, because it brings them great happiness.
And if the target of their love isn't you... then you must relinquish your feelings for the sake of their happiness.
But... that's... so sensible and mature!
I'm far too petty to think like that, ordinarily.
(And according to Quince, so is Othello, in reality...)
You're a little wiser than you look, humble barkeep.
He's right, though. Hamlet owes me nothing.
Whatever's going on in his mind, he clearly has thought little of me lately.
Then you should think only of yourself, too.
Find someone new to love.
Oh, that's all right, Rosie. You know I only ever really have eyes for you, in the end.
And I for you, my little shadow.
Cheers. I'll drink to that.
To new love!
To forgetting old love!
And to friendship!
Old man, oughtn't you to be on duty?
Aye! I could ask you the same, hag.
This is why yer supper-stew always smells like 'alf a casket of wine, ain't it? Yer down here drinking!

Well, well! An' here I thought we were friends.
You? Bah. Never.
What are you doin' here anyhow?
Came to see m' gran'daughter. The babe's not a babe any longer. She's walkin' now.
You have children?
Thirteen of 'em!

She had t'older ones watch th'younger ones, an' all of them tilled the land an' ran the household.
She wos a lot like you, come t'think of it. A real bag o' nails.
Mind your tongue. There's still enough lady left in me to be offended.
How old is the youngest child now?
Fourteen. She's gone an' gotten married, too. Makin' her father proud.
That's Anna. My oldest, Alexander, 'e's got grey at 'is temples, just like me.
Alexander? As in...

The greatest, and the cruelest. Where d'you think Hamlet an' Claudius got their mean streak?
Ah, Alexander beat 'em without a second thought if they weren't polished an' hardy at all times!
But yeh know, he applied that same work to all th'men who served 'im in the wars. Myself included.
It made us all th'better. We were made o' steel! We fought like hell! We sent our enemies packin' a dozen times.

King Alexander sure knew how to discipline 'em like the best. I wos proud to name my son after 'im.
Such a pity and a shame to see his grandson behaving as he does. I wonder what King Alexander would say.
Well, yeh know. Even the best tree produces a weird-lookin' fruit now an' then.
A weird-looking fruit, indeed, that one.
What o' yourself? Where are yer children now?
My husband died not long after I discovered I was with child. He fell under a horse cart and was trampled.
But I swore to build a great family, to move forward even as I prayed for his immortal soul.
I bore my daughter. Marie.
She was a sickly little thing. Hardly the size of my hand when she was born. And she didn't cry.
I thought that made her a peaceful child. I remember marveling to the doctor--'isn't she a wonder, my quiet child?'
But it was bad, the silence. It meant her lungs were weak. She made a faint rattling sound when she breathed.
The night Marie was born, Her Majesty Gertrude was born as well. Little Gerta, they called her.
Gertrude was a healthy child, but her mother made no milk. So they brought her to me.
I fed her and Marie at the same time, looking down at both their faces as I held them close.
Gerta cooed and smiled, and her eyes were curious, even then.
But my daughter Marie—she looked at nothing. She refused my breast. She moved little.
I watched one babe wither away and the other flourish.
One morning, I reached for my daughter, and her tiny body was cold. I called a priest.
They took her from me and buried her.
And I continued to feed Gerta, little Gerta, who grew larger every day.
And now Gerta is grown and married, every bit the graceful woman I knew she would become.
Aw, hell, Irma. I had no clue.
Yeh know...
If it makes yeh feel any better, you can steal all o' my money th'next time we play cards.
Hmm. The despairing look on all of your fat, ruddy faces when I fleece you does bring me great comfort.
Well, now, let's not get ahead o' ourselves, yeh evil hag.
Better evil than a clod.
'Ey, I'm proud t'be a clod. Bein' smart never did anyone no good.
Look at us. Two drunken old fools trading insults. We both have better places to be.
Eh. I'd rather stay here an' drink with you. I'll let Bernardo lecture me later.
Then... cheers. To the old, forgotten ones.
My spring, my joy, my day, my beloved, my laughing rose...
My delight, my wine, my tavern, my lamp, my light, my candle...
And what have we here, Othello?
Ah, just a flight of fancy. The thing's out of tune.
Sounds tuned well enough to me.
And I do so love to be serenaded. Especially by the strong, silent type.
Me? Silent? You must be joking.
Hmm. Excellent point. Strong, then.
What would you like to hear?
Oh, there's a little old bit of something I heard in the barracks often...
The barracks? You, a soldier?
Ahh, believe it or not... once. Under King Hamlet in his infamous three-year chess match with Norway.
Three years is but a blink of an eye in a war, back where I come from.
When the countries are but a week's travel apart, a three-year conflict feels like eternity.
But I wasn't cut out for that life, I'm afraid. I much prefer reasonable discussion to endless posturing and saber-rattling.
And I much prefer to rattle a literal saber.
You have the look of an old soldier about you. In which war did you fight?
Which war? Why, the unending war the Turks wage upon all who do not bow to the Sultan.
I served at the Sultan's pleasure for over a decade and fought for his causes against foreigners. I beheaded thousands of men.
I find that strangely charming. And possibly seductive.
Hmph. Well, I'm certain there's many a man willing to... grab your head around here.
Toward the end of my decade, I was one of the Sultan's own viziers. I had gardens and treasures aplenty. This feels like a different world entirely.
You gave up all that to come to this rotten, pasty little country? Why on earth?
Because it was not truly mine. I was an Ottoman slave. Everything I did was in my master's name, even when I surpassed his rank with my own.
In fact, my master's name—'Halil'—was appended to my name quite literally. I longed to be my own man. So I fled.
I imagine you aren't welcome in Constantinople any longer.
I'm sure they would welcome me. Right into an execution chamber.
Heh. Well, with the way Denmark's trending, your fortunes may not be better here.
Aye. What a pity, that.
...At least we've still got music.
It is the only thing which transcends language or border.
Even dance may offend. But music is immortal.
I wish you excellent fortune in getting that lute to tune.
Thanks, friend. We'll see.
The time has come, my noble ladies. Hop to it.
T-t-this is exploitation!
Yes! This is humane!
You mean inhumane, Guilda.
That's what I said!
Need I remind you the sum of your debt to me?
Five years of losing every game you've played at my table. Plus interest.
I must be repaid, if I have to rip those fine dresses off you two and sell them!
We helped you find your ingredients earlier!
Feh! You think that is enough to make up your sum? Hardly!
It's true we've failed to pay Irma in the past...
But I must admit, I'd assumed she would have forgotten.
N-not to mention, I thought we'd have skipped town by now.
This was supposed to be a quick visit. Pay our respects and leave!
Enough! Now! Begin!
Ugh! Fine!
(You sing. I'll provide, er, emotional support.)
(Why am I always the singer?!)
D-deathless Aphrodite, throned in flowers...
Break my spirit, Lady, no longer!
Hear anew the voice! O hear and listen!
Come, as in that island dawn thou camest...
From thy father's golden house, hearing my pleading!
Uhm, how does the rest of it go?
You stood with a sudden brilliance, Goddess, before me...
You asked me what I suffered, who was my cause of anguish...
'Now she runs away, but she'll soon pursue you;'
'Gifts she now rejects, soon she'll give them...'
'Now she doesn't love you, but soon her heart will burn...'
Come to me again and abate my torment!
Give me what I long for!
Guilda, what song is that?
I have absolutely no idea.
It just sort of came to me. You know?
I guess Aphrodite really is my muse!
What in black hell was that? I asked you to play something that would attract a paying audience!
And that's exactly what we did. Look at all of these admiring fans!
We've attracted quite the crowd, it's true.
You idiots. They're only here because they think you're going to take off your skirts.
What? Why would they think that?
Ah, well, that verse you chose...
It's a little—shall we say—romantic?
Well, of course. That's the only sort of verse worth knowing.
You two are a lost cause. A sunk cost. I'll never see a single coin of my money, will I?
I've had enough. I'm returning to the castle.
Well, there goes our last chance to ever deal in at Irma's table again.
There, there. It's all right. She's a cheat anyhow, and we both knew it.
We'll simply have to find some other way to entertain ourselves in this dreadful place, I suppose.
I can think of a few ways you can entertain each other!
Aye! Take 'er sleeves down!
We'll pay yeh!
Y-you're all vile!
Yeah! Shame on you! Our love is not for sale!
Wait. What?
Nothing, nothing. Rosie, let's get out of here!
She's got a lovely sound.
Mm. First lute I ever bought. I've given it a touch-up and it's like new now.
Thought I'd follow a lark or two.
What's yours made of? Such a fascinating surface.
No name you would recognize. It was made in my homeland.
Where are you from?
Same as you, from the looks of it.
You're mistaken, sir.
Some parts of you seem Danish, to a degree. Your fine clothes mark you a part of the local flock.
My sister and I were born here.
Ah. Then by reputation, you are that one they call Lord Laertes.
I've seen your father. Pale little man. So I must admit, you fascinate me.
You're not the first to be curious. If you must know, my mother was a foreigner.
Of course. Hard to imagine she wouldn't be.
What was it like, living with a father like that?
He wanted—wants—to protect us. Sometimes that protection became unbearable.
Often, as a boy, I would ask him why we looked strange, my sister and I. He always feigned confusion.
And his feigned confusion frightened me. I wondered if he didn't truly see that we were different.
Because... others did.
I've been called every horrid thing under the sun, in whispered breath or behind a lifted palm.
Sometimes, when I wander through town, I'll find a stone skidded against my leg from afar, or hear the jeering of children.
But I am who I am. I refuse to hide.
Oh, yes. I'm well familiar.
We draw quite a crowd, don't we? But where there's numbers, there's strength.
And there's fear.
Look around. Everyone's leaving the bar.
That'll be my doing, I'm afraid.
Well. Those same townsfolk drop coins into my till every night by the dozen to have me pour their beer.
They may be nervous now, but they'll be back tonight. This is the cheapest place they can drink. And then—my bar, my rules.
So much as the smallest smirk or slur is dropped, they're out of my establishment forever. By my own hand.
I cannot promise that the world outside is kind, my lord.
But in here, things are different. At least for now.
If you would ever come to play by the fire a while, you would be in good hands and good company.
Bring your own lute next time. We'll play a ditty or three together.
You have my thanks. I shall consider the offer most intently.
Claudius and Hamlet ran to the chapel. They looked upset. I ought to pay them a visit.
Ah. Ophelia. You're back at last.
I'd heard your ship was returned to port...
And so was yours, it seems.
Ophelia. I've returned.
So soon? Oughtn't you to be in Paris by now?
I was at port in Aalborg when I heard the news. About everything happening back here, that is.
The situation in Elsinore has deteriorated quickly.
Are you all right? No one's harmed you?
I'm safe, for now.
There's work to be done, and I intend to act swiftly.
Good. Then there's work to be done, and I intend to act swiftly.
Father wrote me a letter, you know. He explained everything.
About Hamlet's attempt on his life. I doubt that Hamlet could have acted alone.
And what do you intend to do about it?
Ensure no one can ever threaten my family again.
In the wake of his death, I have to imagine Hamlet acting against Father was not his own doing. Someone spurred him.
I intend to raise arms against this sea of troubles.
I heard about what happened to Father. How Hamlet brutalized him.
But I cannot believe Hamlet acted alone. Someone spurred him.
Even with Hamlet dead, the matter is not handled. And I intend to pursue it to its root.
Father's gone, but we're still here. I'm concerned about your safety in all this.
I heard about the circumstances around Hamlet's death.
I've come back to understand. And to sort through what's left.
That is to say, here, by the fire. I'm not ready to return to Elsinore just yet.
Thank you for coming swiftly. He's gone too far this time, Bernardo. Hamlet, I mean.
Threatening Father's life-- he nearly killed the man.
You were there, were you not? I heard you rendered Hamlet unconscious. Prevented further bloodshed.
I was. I am uncertain what would have transpired had your sister not alerted me to the situation.
That's why this has to end. I need you to help me, old friend.
Will you ensure Hamlet is properly contained and brought to justice?
I don't mean rotting in a cell. I mean gone. For good.
He's gone to England. What would you have me do? Hasn't he been punished sufficiently?
No. I want him dead, no matter whose soil he walks on. I know your family must have some connections.
Laertes, I'm afraid it is not so simple.
For all that Hamlet is not in his right mind as of late, the incident with your father was an accident.
He believed his uncle was behind the curtain in the Queen's bedroom, spying on him.
He never intended your father any direct harm. It was horrific, yes, but not a meditated act.
Surely you cannot mean...
That you intend to let Hamlet walk free as a result?
At this stage, I fear having Hamlet executed would only exacerbate the tension in Elsinore, not improve it.
It appeared to be a regrettable incident, but a one-time incident nonetheless.
You-- you're my best friend. The man whose heart I believed in most ardently.
How can you stand here and defend my father's attacker?
You understand the great love I bear for you and your family, Laertes. Always have. Always will.
I am the Captain of the Guard. It is not my place to mete out punishment and retribution and righteous judgement.
It is my place to keep as many people alive as I possibly can, and to maintain the sanctity of the state of Denmark.
You're a man of God. Isn't it said in Matthew, 'An eye for an eye, and tooth for tooth'?
Of course. But that is only the first line of that passage.
'...But I say unto you, that ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.'
It continues, 'Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you.'
I will not stand here and let Hamlet threaten all I hold dear.
If you won't stop him, rest assured that if he ever sets foot on Danish soil again, I will. Farewell.
If you won't stop him, rest assured, I will. Farewell.
You summoned me, my lord?
Ah. Polonius. Come in.
So. Laertes is staying in Elsinore indefinitely, at least for the time being.
What are your thoughts on the matter?
At first I was concerned, but now I find something rather timely in it.
Well. The mood has certainly shifted in the castle suddenly, don't you think?
So much has happened in such a short time.
Mmm. I see.
Polonius, do you often play chess?
I must admit, I haven't quite kept my tactician's instincts sharp! Fancy a match?
Of course, of course. I used to be quite the thorn in your brother's side, you know.
Don't think he beat me a single game in the last three years of his life--Hoh!
And that's after his chess tutor from Naples was through with him.
Let's test your mettle, then. I'll give you first move.
As always, I open with a pawn to center.
And so shall I.
Then where from here? Where, indeed. Hmm...
I don't like to play sober, I'll admit. Shall I pour us a drink or two?
But of course, but of course.
Ah, I quite like this opening. And here's my knight.
Hmm. Let me think a moment.
Polonius, why did your son truly cancel his voyage?
Urgh... excuse me. I feel-- it's a little stifling in here, isn't it? Allow me to stand a moment and catch my breath.
Didn't you know I'd hear of his return the minute he stepped foot on the dock? Didn't you think word would carry?
The little conversation he had with that barkeep in town. How angry he seemed. How full of fire.
I don't understand. When did this conversation happen? What barkeep?
Let's drop the pretenses. I know you brought Laertes here to run me out of my own kingdom, or else run me through.
You think to put him on the throne over me. I saw through your move the minute he returned.
My lord, it's so hot in here, my throat is... it's tightening.
Can we not go outside into the fresh air?
No, we can't.
You tried to play me for a fool.
You may think me a doddering, incompetent version of my brother. But allow me to assure you: I am much more.
(I thought I'd saved him. What a fool I am.)
(But if I reveal myself, he'll only kill me, too.)
And unlike him, I'll do whatever vile thing I must in order to keep my country.
What a shame it is, that you should pass away in such an undignified manner.
(T-that vial--Where is it?)
Something amiss, my lord?
No. Nothing at all. Only... you must excuse me, Polonius.
I've just remembered I promised to meet with someone here in a moment.
It's a private meeting.
Ah. I... see. I'll take my leave, then.
Yes, I think that's wise.
Guards! Guards, to me, to me!
My King? What's happened?
How... who ransacked my personal belongings?
Someone must know. About me. About my brother.
Lord Polonius collapsed during our game. He's not breathing.
I shouldn't be here. They'll find me.
I shouldn't be here. He'll find me.
Lady Ophelia. Surely you've seen her?
Guildenstern. She slipped away at some point, and I cannot find her.
Please, will you watch for me? If you see her, tell me.
It's-- it's extraordinarily unusual for her to not tell me where she's gone.
The last time it happened... was when Hamlet spurned her, years ago. I almost lost her then.
But this must be something else. Something she never told me. I'm afraid.
I-- I don't mean to trouble you. I apologize. I'll take my leave of you now.
What brings you down here, my lord?
Something delicate.
I have a favor to ask of you.
And what are you asking me to take care of now?
I'm ordering you to keep it private.
It's something my wife cannot know about. Not yet. Not now. I'll tell her, but in my own time.
I fear with the state she's in, this letter would only send her reeling into the abyss.
You've threatened me in the past. What makes you believe I have any obligation to be discreet?
Because of the love you bear for my wife, I should hope.
This would be the end of her. Think on that, and keep this among your belongings.
Do your men have a particular habit of snooping in your things?
They each understand the kind of severe and unrelenting punishment I would levy on them.
It's safe here, for now.
Wah hah hah! That's the Bernardo I know.
Good. It's settled, then. I'll return to you in time, when I'm ready to show her what's written inside.
Father. I've come to take you from this place.
Unlock the door.
What's happening? Who's there? I can hardly see.
Allow me to help you out, Lord Polonius.
Has the King determined my fate?
Claudius? Truly? Then why are you here?
I did not believe the King's order to imprison you was done in good faith, or out of a genuine need for security.
It appeared he did this simply to punish you. In light of his passing, I would like to restore you to a place of dignity.
Of course, I will still expect your compliance in all matters of state. But for now, you are free.
Thank you. Thank you all.
Laertes, please have the servants bring food and water. I have felt such a chill these last few days. All my strength has left me.
God's wounds, I thought I would die in there.
Suspected I might find you here.
I heard a little something from Ophelia, and had the thought to seek you out.
A 'little something?' Very discriminating of you to reveal your source!
I want to ask about you and Hamlet. I rather suspect you won't want to be asked, which only makes the asking more worthwhile.
Your assessment is correct.
I understand some of this may be painful for you now that Hamlet's gone.
But I also know-- or suspect-- that you are not someone who collapses under his grief.
Correct again.
As I recall, you remained close to his side for quite a long time, didn't you?
After all, when Guildenstern and I met you, Hamlet had already been at school for a year. And your presence in his life predated that.
When did you first begin following him around?
You make me sound like a little lap dog.
Aren't you?
I began following Hamlet after the last war with Norway came to its conclusion, when Hamlet's father drove his blade through Fortinbras the Elder's heart.
I was a soldier then, but never fancied myself a career military man.
Too much work. Not enough job security. And a poor use of my excellent taste in food, wine, and art.
King Hamlet, seeing that I was something of a learned man, made a request of me.
Hamlet was to be educated at Wittenberg soon. But Hamlet's father was worried about him.
Of course, you remember what Hamlet was like before his father's death.
He was wild in a different sort of way then. I remember him diving nude into the Elbe river in midwinter.
And then he called out to us to join him...
Which of course we were never going to do. What was he thinking?
None of us ever really knew. And now it's too late to find out.
That's really Hamlet in a nut shell. One never knows what he's thinking.
So King Hamlet sent you along to Wittenberg to watch over Hamlet. Is that it?
Yes. That's it.
Unlike other trusted men in the King's employ, Hamlet and I were not so dissimilar in age that it would appear strange for me to accompany him.
And Hamlet was well aware of my role. He and I disliked one another immensely at first. I found him far too bold a flavor for my tastes, and he found my very presence stifling.
But over time, we developed a healthy respect for one another. That respect became trust, and that trust became friendship.
Just friendship?
What are you implying?
I want to leave no room for misinterpretation. After all, in many places, your mere insinuations could have me executed.
Horatio, you ought to know me better than that. How many of my lady loves did you meet at Wittenberg?
That's why I'm here. I knew I needed to speak with you if no one else would.
So that's what this is about.
Fine. If you must hear it, let me say it, then. I came to love Hamlet.
I've never said it to anyone else, least of all to him.
And now I never shall.
And he spent all these years not knowing?
Well, I wouldn't say that. Just that I've never said the words.
There was... one evening. The both of us were staggeringly drunk. And the night got away from us, so to speak.
I thought--
I thought to myself the next morning: If he cares for you as you do him, he'll say something.
But he never did.
And so, neither did I. And the silence just sort of stretched all these years.
You've been carrying the weight of something like this all alone. It must have been heavy.
Have you ever thought of sharing it with him?
I-- I have. But I am afraid, in my heart of hearts.
His life is full of so much darkness right now. He's in the worst place I've ever seen him. How can I contribute to that?
Horatio, I'm no expert when it comes to matters of social finesse, as you've no doubt witnessed. But there's one thing I know for certain.
You cannot shoulder this burden forever, waiting for a 'right moment' which may never arrive.
You've got to be earnest with Hamlet. What is it they say? Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.
I have been afraid of this too long, and for what reason?
I never thought myself a man who avoided the difficult conversations.
So you'll speak with him?
If my lady suggests it.
Then who am I to refuse?
Thank you, Rosencrantz.
Any time. Any time at all. I hope the conversation runs to its due course.
I-- I have. But something happened to him recently. I don't know that he even sees me when he looks at me, right now.
His mind's fully gone.
Then-- don't carry this alone. Let me carry it with you.
Guilda and I are going to depart Elsinore soon. Circumstances being what they are, it simply feels like the right time to move on.
Won't you come with us?
I-- I suppose I could. This place holds no meaning to me anymore without him.
Where will you go?
We've no idea. We never do. Perhaps we'll go somewhere a little warmer to shake the chill that's descended here.
That's all I needed to hear.
Consider me intrigued. But give me time to think upon it.
I think it took saying all this out loud to understand for myself what I needed to do.
You have my thanks for being the echo I needed.
Any time.
Let me carry it with you.
Guilda and I are going to depart Elsinore soon, now that Hamlet's gone.
Mind an interruption?
From you? Never.
I see. Excellent. I have something to-- ah-- to discuss with you.
What's wrong? You're trembling.
Has some new horror taken place?
No. No, it's nothing like that.
I wanted to ask you about the past. There's something that's been on my mind for quite a while now.
Do you remember that night in Wittenberg, during that first year?
Perhaps. It all feels so distant now. What night do you mean?
I think you know precisely what I mean. And I don't think either of us can hide from it anymore.
Horatio, you're talking nonsense. I don't remember that night.
Let's go inside, shall we?
Wait. Don't run from this. Please.
This is all so serious! Must it be so serious? Why? Why can't we leave what happened in the past?
Because I need to understand.
I think you know what I'm about to say.
I've been in love with you for a long time, Hamlet.
Haven't you got anything to say in response?
I... I don't know. This is sudden.
Let's say that I did remember what happened that evening.
Have I ever given you any indication of inappropriate feelings since then?
Hamlet, what would be inappropriate about feelings like that?
I don't know, exactly. But I know that whatever happened between us, I have put it to rest in the echoes of the past.
And I don't think I ever had the capacity to feel whatever it is you're feeling now.
Then that's the answer to my question. We needn't belabor the point further.
I know what it's like to love someone who doesn't care for you.
I know how painful that is. And if that's how you've been feeling all this time, then it must be agonizing.
I am far too old to agonize over unrequited love. Lingering disappointment, on the other hand, is not beyond me.
Of course this isn't the answer I wanted to hear. But it's the answer I have.
I do love you in a way. But it isn't like that, and it never will be.
Maybe... if I weren't who I am... if I weren't a Prince of Denmark... maybe things would be different.
But what I am is solid, by circumstance of my birth. I can be no other man. And it means that some pieces of me must remain locked away forever.
I will always be your most ardent and faithful friend. But when it comes to matters of love, that's different.
You deserve someone who isn't me, Horatio.
So that's it, then. That's how this ends.
Somehow I thought it'd be more than that. I played that conversation in my head a thousand times.
And in the end, I had my answer in just a scant few minutes.
I've a new wound to nurse.
But still, I sense that this wound will heal faster.
And when it heals, perhaps finally it will be healed for good.
You have returned.
King Hamlet? Surely that can't be you.
It is.
It's been a long time.
Has it?
Or at least, I think-- I think I've been gone a long time.
It felt like an instant between the last time I saw you and this awakening, now. I suppose I must have been waiting for you, then.
It's good to see you. We make an odd pair, don't we? But I've got some unfinished business.
Evidently so.
Say, there isn't a mirror in here. What do I look like?
My hands-- they're so soft!
You look just as you did then.
It's a funny thing, these young, delicate hands. I spent the rest of my life not knowing how strong these hands already were.
Glad to see death hasn't sapped you of your steel.
Of course not. Where are we? When are we?
This is the afterwards. Neither Heaven nor Hell. Simply the nothingness in between.
I came here for a reason, I think.
I have to go back to Elsinore.
Go back?
Can you help me? Do you still know how to return?
Of course I do. But why would you consider such a thing?
After all this time...
You chose, Ophelia!
You left that world behind. Why now?
What if I chose wrong?
What difference does that make?
An entire lifetime of difference!
And a difference in the lives of all those people. What if there's a different world, a better world? Don't I owe them that?
Ophelia. Do you know what I would give to have left Elsinore behind in life, even just once?
That chance was stolen from me.
Now you treat it as though it's something easily exchanged. As though you could put your life back on the shelf and choose another.
I know it's painful. I'm sorry to have woken you again. I wanted to let you rest-- I didn't know coming back would be like this.
You know I'd never intend to hurt you, Hamlet.
Truth be told, I'm not even certain I should be re-opening the Book of Fates.
If I cannot find another fate worth pursuing, I may simply let the matter rest and return to the world I had chosen after all.
I can always return here, can I not?
No, no. There is something you do not understand about the threads of fate, I think. They are woven together as one, a transcendent tapestry.
This is not a simple matter of browsing what might have been.
By choosing the world you did, you pulled that world's thread forever. If you choose to return to Elsinore, you cannot return to the path you chose.
You're saying...
Yes. In other words, you will not be able to return to that particular fate.
It is shattered. Gone. And once you set foot back in Elsinore, you will lose all memory of what you chose.
Please. I urge you not to do this, Ophelia. I urge you with everything in my heart.
It's not too late to turn back!
Disregard King Hamlet's words and return to Elsinore?
Here you are yet again.
Perhaps. Perhaps not.
What do you recall?
Only that I came here at the end of my life. And I know now-- though I did not know in Elsinore-- that you and I have spoken here before, in this place.
This... in-between.
And what before that? What before we last spoke?
I cannot remember.
Then it is as I warned you. You have no memory of the fate you chose before.
That must be true.
Still, I think I returned to this place because I have to go back to Elsinore.
You already have.
And evidently, I didn't find what I was looking for.
Yes. Your return on that occasion brought you no more happiness than your first fate.
What leads you to believe that this attempt shall yield more fruitful results?
Besides, if you return to Elsinore again, you will lose all memory of this fate, too.
This past time... when you chose your fate... that me, that Hamlet, had no knowledge of this in-between place. Neither did you.
That version of me believed we were still friends. But now, looking at you, my wits about me, I am not so certain.
You need not continue, you know. Will you finally allow all of us to rest?
Or will you force the both of us to continue to endure this hell?
I had thought you'd surely not return.
I thought the same.
You know, I cherish you dearly when I am pulled back to Elsinore.
I have no memory of this place, this in-between.
Then I am brought back here when you die, and I remember you chose to return me to Elsinore too, and it aches so terribly.
I'm forcing you to wake up again every time I do this, aren't I?
And this is the third time.
But I can remember living only one fate. Only the last.
Say, Hamlet-- what were those other fates I chose?
Were they-- was I-- happier?
I suspected you would find yourself wondering this.
But I do not know. I do not see your life beyond Elsinore. I am not a god. Just a man, or what was once a man, standing here as confused as you.
Please, Ophelia.
Do not return to Elsinore again.
If ever you did love me, if ever you did find me worthy of your time... then you will join me here in the quiet of oblivion, and take up an eternal rest.
You know I do, Hamlet.
But I must have returned here for a reason. I think my work in Elsinore is not yet complete.
It will never be complete.
I urge you to understand this!
I harbored a deep and impenetrable respect for you in life, Ophelia. Do not prove me a fool in death.
Do not show me that everything we went through together was trivial compared to your pining for the impossible.
If you return to Elsinore again, you will again lose all memory of the fate you just chose, and you will not be able to choose it again. In other words...
I have a rather unpleasant choice to make, it seems.
You are no better than him, you know.
You have shown me already that, like him, you will not grant mercy.
We are simply playthings to you.
I must remind you, as you abandon the fate you last chose...
Let me give you what you desire, then. The chance to find something else. Something 'better.'
Let me give you what you came here for. We have nothing more to say to one another, after all.
I've already made my decision. I want to return to Elsinore.
I'm sorry, Hamlet.
I never thought you were quite this stubborn in life.
Nevertheless, I will show you the way back to Elsinore.
I would be a fool not to listen to you.
You have my eternal thanks.
You are wiser and more merciful than that broken world ever deserved.
Let us go away now, Ophelia. Forever.
Couldn't agree more, my friend. Wherever we are...
I think we've both earned that sleep of death, and whatever dreams may come.
I must return to Elsinore again.
I know nothing I could say would make it any less of a cruelty.
I mourn the fate you leave behind, for certainly neither you nor I will recall it if we ever meet again.
I've already made my decision. I want to return to Elsinore again. A third time.
I'm sorry, Hamlet. I truly am.
So be it. I hope we never meet again, then.
And if we ever do, I shall no longer try to stand in your way.
Trying to save someone from pain is a courtesy one only extends to friends.
Wherever we are...
Your time with Grace-- the adventures you embarked on-- will vanish.
That sacrifice you made for the sake of others will have been meaningless, for there is no such similar path.
Your memory of the time you spent with Laertes and your father, both the good and bad, will vanish.
You will never again have the power to overturn nations at your whim. At least-- not in the same way.
You will never again live out the rest of your life at Hamlet's side.
That perfect world you created will shatter. And I will warn you now: No other fate you could choose could possibly live up to its happiness.
You will never again be able to guarantee that everyone in Elsinore survives.
You will forego the life you and Othello built together. And without leaving Elsinore with you, he is likely to be killed here.
You will never again have a future you built away from Elsinore, on your own, free of others' misery.
Never again will you settle down with Lady Guildenstern and Lady Rosencrantz, though you had found peace with them.
There is no other world with such a peaceful existence for Elsinore as the one where Fortinbras was its true King.

Hamlet and I were together for two years, in secret. In that time, he was... different. Happier. He had a sense of humor then. Neither of us had ever loved another before, but he treated me with respect and an unfailing kindness.

When the King was young, his older brother used to beat him severely, and he spent much of his life afraid of Hamlet. Is it any wonder Claudius despises young Hamlet, the spitting image of his tormentor?
My father is so loyal to the King that he's still keeping secrets on the King's behalf after King Hamlet's death. I worry it's going to bring Father nothing but trouble in the long term.
I managed to save Father's life. It seems that anytime Hamlet is distracted or prevented from meeting his mother after the play, Father is safe.

Father goes to visit Mother's grave often. He still mourns her all the time. He tells me she'd be proud of the person I became. I hope that's true. I don't remember her, so all I know of her is what Father and Laertes tell me. Can you love someone you don't remember?
I've learned that Laertes will choose to stay in Elsinore if he believes that going to Paris might expose someone he cares about to danger.

I recently uncovered that my brother and Lady Brit are involved romantically, and have been for quite some time. It's understandable they want to keep the relationship a secret, given the various political pressures at play. I, er... stumbled in on them by mistake.

I recently uncovered that my brother and Brit are involved romantically, and have been for quite some time. It's understandable they want to keep the relationship a secret, given the various political pressures at play. I, er... stumbled in on them by mistake.

When it came down to sacrificing me or standing against the orders of every man above her, Brit tried to save me. All it took was getting to know her. Whatever our relationship was before, I know this now: Brit is not my enemy. She might even be my greatest ally.
Brit has no desire to be here at Elsinore; she seems deeply unhappy, as though something's weighing heavily upon her. Maybe it's time I got to know her better.

I saw Bernardo performing in town today, as Katherine. I never knew. We grew up together, and I never knew. This doesn't change my feelings towards Bernardo, however she or he chooses to live in the future—but for now, the Bernardos in other worlds would clearly prefer to keep this information private.

Bernardo is Catholic, and prays in the mornings sometimes. He's deeply private about his faith, especially in light of the recent burnings of churches around the country. His father was also a religious man.
Horatio is religious, but he isn't Catholic or Lutheran. He called himself a 'heathen,' and claimed to worship 'devas' and 'asuras.' I'm not sure what that means.
Thanks to me, Irma's quest to kick up a regular game of cards has finally succeeded. I hope she doesn't get in too much trouble with Bernardo when he inevitably finds out.

I learned that Irma had a daughter and a husband once. But that was a long time ago. The child died while she served as wet nurse for Gertrude. That must be why she feels such an incredible drive to protect her.

Quince is a traveling player who occasionally comes to put on productions at Elsinore Castle. He writes and performs all of his own material, often on short notice. I recall he was rather close once with the late King Hamlet, and was a favorite performer of his.
Quince is somehow stuck outside the flow of time, like me. He's offered me his assistance in solving my way out of my own quandary. I hope I can ask him about anything I might encounter.

I see. Quince isn't just repeating time along with me. He also seems to have some small ability to alter the flow of events. But if that's true, then why doesn't he just... alter his way out? Is he here for my sake?

When I found Quince in the gallery, he spoke in riddles. Something about the nature and structure of a tragic work. Of course I've read many of the great tragedies-- and it sometimes feels like I'm living one-- but what does all that have to do with my predicament?
Marcellus has thirteen children, and grandchildren at that. I had no idea he was so-- er-- prolific. Then again, having to raise thirteen children would explain why nothing fazes him.

I found King Hamlet's abandoned notes describing the end of his life. He was like me. But he gave up, and let madness consume him. He knew and understood everything that was happening around him-- his brother's plot against him, his wife turning from him-- and he couldn't stop it. Now he remains in Elsinore, neither alive nor fully dead. But why? Will that happen to me, too?

King Hamlet appeared before me one final time. He told me that there will be no true ending, no right ending. There is no such thing as happiness. All that remains is my power to choose. He urged me to use it wisely. He said that whatever I do, I must use it. Not simply give up, as he did. And... he called me... his friend.
A New Beginning
I've woken up in my bed again, but things feel - different. Strange.
My father was waiting, as usual, but not to chastise me -- rather, to invite me to some sort of feast in the Great Hall. I'll need to join everyone there.
I'd forgotten what it was like to see them all happy. This world -- this new world -- is this the world that would have been without the Book of Fates, without any of it?
Laertes is late
someone heard a report
Hamlet is staying
Hrm. I should probably check on the meal.
This fire is—wahh! Hot! Hot! Too hot!
Look at you, Irma, dancing around like a village idiot!
Have some dignity!—But ooh, that pan...
Nothing but the walls and the chapel this way.
Father said Laertes was meeting with the King, did he not? He wouldn't be back there.
No one is on the walls right now. I should look somewhere else.
The King and Queen's private chambers are up that way. Laertes won't be up there.
Guard Captain Bernardo, give me your report.
Better give me the report again, Bernardo.
The Prince of Norway demands we surrender the north.
Surrender to Fortinbras? Hah! The balls of a stallion, that young prince!
Fortinbras claims the late King Hamlet, rest his soul, won those swamplands unjustly from his father.
My brother won them for Denmark, certainly, but with all the fairness afforded to war.
He can shed all the tears he likes for that swampland. I won't bother to hear his complaints.
Yes, my lord. We'll send our reply.
Dearest, what will we do if Fortinbras wages war on our lands regardless?
We'll fight him head-on. He's an impetuous young boy—no more threat than a gadfly to our throne, my love.
That's how my brother would have done it!
May he rest in peace.
Yes, yes, my brother's passed—but now is a time for Denmark's new glory. Now is the time for us to expand.
With my lovely Queen by my side, we will be a force far beyond anything the northern lands have seen before!
Prince Fortinbras will not retreat easily. He is hot-headed—as his father was. He has a temper, my lord.
Are you questioning my ability to provide for Denmark's battle plan when the time comes, Guard Captain Bernardo?
Not at all, my lord. Merely... suggesting.
My lord... I tire of this. And besides, I believe young Laertes must meet his father's beckon.
My wife is right. We've had enough of political affairs for now. Today is a day for celebration, after all!
Young Prince Fortinbras grows beyond his leash. We ought to engage not with him, but with his uncle, the true King of Norway.
Bernardo, have Voltimand deliver a message to the King with our terms.
At once, milord.
Now then. Laertes, Hamlet? Please come forward.
I've been given word that the both of you wish to have my formal permission to leave Denmark.
My King, I want to travel to Paris tomorrow morning, that I might learn about the breadth of life's offerings beyond Danish walls.
And I want to return to Wittenberg, because—I agree—these Danish walls are absolutely miserable.
I have some concerns about each of you. You are yet young men. Laertes, what does your father say?
He is worried, my King, but grants his blessing.
Then I must concede. Hamlet, on the other hand...
Your mother the Queen and I would prefer you near to us, Hamlet. You may not go back to Germany.
The funeral for my brother is two months past, and yet you still wear black!
I wear mourning attire while I still mourn my father.
The time for that has passed. You ought to think of me as your father now—your father the King. Nothing has changed.
For your own health, I desire that you stay in Denmark.
If that's your wish, Uncle.
As is customary, I have no choice. I never do.
Excellent! All is settled. And with that, let us break a little while. Court is dismissed.
Thank you, my lord! Thank you!
You are most welcome, Laertes. Swift travels, my boy!
Ophelia—whenever you are done here, come meet me outside. I've something I want to tell you before I meet with Father.
TEMP: You shouldn't see this! I am too busy to talk to anyone!
Ophelia! There you are, love.
And, as usual, doesn't even give me so much as a 'Hello, Father.'
Hello, Father.
That's better. And what are you doing all the way out here?
I wanted to be alone a while. It's quiet here.
Avoiding me, more like. Well, I've a small favor to ask of you.
Your brother's in the throne room, visiting the King about his voyage. But His Majesty tends to run overlong...
Won't you fetch Laertes for me? Tell him he's tardy. As usual, his trunks are sitting in his chambers, open and empty.
At this rate, he'll go to Paris with nothing but the clothes on his back!
That would come as no surprise to either of us.
Of course not.
Much as I try, I cannot help but think of how terribly I'll miss him.
And with all that's going on here in Denmark... war brewing, and such...
I think my hair has gotten a little whiter even as we stand here. The nerves are taking quite a toll on me.
Father, go and have a stroll. Breathe. I'll fetch Laertes.
This is why you're my favorite daughter.
Only daughter.
And that as well!
That meeting... we'd been in there an hour. You've freed me. Eternally grateful.
I sensed you needed rescuing, even though I know you've been waiting for a return to ordinary affairs.
It's refreshing, no? After the dark cloud that's descended on Elsinore lately...
The last few months certainly have been odd.
What was it you wanted to discuss, then?
You know, Ophelia... I'm going to miss you.
And I you, brother.
You and Prince Hamlet... you're not... anymore...?
Hamlet and I aren't... together anymore, Laertes. I swear it on Mother's grave.
Has he given you any trouble?
No. He's far more focused on glaring daggers at his Uncle Claudius.
How long has it been since his father's funeral? A month? Two? And yet he scarcely seems to have recovered.
King Hamlet could do no wrong in his son's eyes, I'm certain. No doubt Hamlet's grief has been overwhelming as of late.
And Hamlet hates his uncle for marrying his mother. I see the way he looks at him. His eyes...
Like a kicked dog, angry, fuming, unpredictable.
It is both proper and customary that Gertrude married her husband's brother after her husband's death. I've no idea why Hamlet's in a fit about it.
It has me worried he might take out his anger upon you.
Laertes. You needn't throw shoes any more.
Throw shoes?
You remember when we were small, that one summer when that baroness and her children came to visit Elsinore?
You mean those horrible little boys who pushed you down?
Yes. And when one of them pulled my hair and said it looked odd--
Ah. Right. I'd forgotten. I threw my boot at him.
And you've been doing it ever since.
No one pushes my sister around. Well, unless it's me, of course.
They won't. That's what I'm telling you. I can fend for myself now. I promise.
I'm not that little girl anymore. And I'm not going to let anyone do harm to me.
I suppose that's true, isn't it?
You really have changed.
I see something of Mother in you, now. She could be fierce like that.
I likely won't see you before I leave tomorrow. But...
My son, I believe you still have some things to attend to?
Your ship leaves tomorrow morning, after all. You have little time to dally.
You're correct. As usual, I've packed nothing at all until the very eve of my departure.
Better throw a few of my best doublets in a trunk and call it a night.
Please get some sleep. You'll need it.
I heard what your brother told you about Prince Hamlet.
He's right. Prince Hamlet's poison to a young woman like you.
And besides that, he's going to inherit the crown someday. It's a delicate situation, that one.
I know you loved him once. I'm your father. I see these things.
I know I ought not to be around him any longer.
For another young noblewoman, things might be different. But not so for you.
These matters become more difficult for you and Laertes.
I'm well aware, Father. We both are.
But I am no scullery maid. I will not be forced to shrink from him.
No. No, I wouldn't dream of asking that. I merely desire your safety.
Of course. I understand, Father.
Smart girl. Sweet dreams.
It's late. I really ought to sleep.
I wish to offer you the advice of an old man, whatever little that's worth to the young.
Laertes, Paris can be a... a... confusing place for a young man like yourself.

But please. Try to sleep more and take excellent care of your health. I worry for you.
